resonance.q: Resonance structures differ only in the position of:
options: The net charge of the molecule

resonance.q: The real structure of a resonance-stabilized species is:
options: Whichever single structure is drawn first
An average (hybrid) of all valid resonance structures
Constantly flipping between structures over time

resonance.q: Which resonance structure generally contributes most to the real hybrid?
options: The one with the most atoms
The one with full octets and minimal formal charge
Whichever has the most double bonds regardless of charge

resonance.q: Resonance structures must all have the same:

Resonance stabilization generally makes a molecule or ion:

More stable than any single contributing structure
Exactly as stable as the average of the contributing structures' energies

resonance.q: Which pair of features makes a resonance structure a poor (minor) contributor?
options: Full octets on all atoms and no charge separation
Negative charge on the more electronegative atom
Positive charge on carbon plus a broken octet
Charges that are close together but opposite in sign

resonance.q: Placing a negative formal charge on oxygen is generally more favorable than placing it on carbon in a resonance structure.
For an allylic cation (CH2=CH–CH2+), the curved arrow used to draw its second resonance structure moves electrons from:

resonance.q: Why does an amide (R–CO–NH2) have a C–N bond that is shorter and stronger than a typical amine C–N bond?

options: They must have the same formal charges on every atom
They must both be neutral overall
They must share connectivity and electron count

Carbonyl carbons have no bonds available

electrophiles.q: Which of these is typically NOT a good electrophile?
Which carbon of ClCH₂–CH₂–CO–CH₃ is the most electrophilic?
options: The middle CH₂ of the chain
The methyl on the far right

electrophiles.q: An electrophile must always carry a full positive formal charge.
Why is the carbon of an epoxide ring a good electrophile even though the molecule overall is neutral?
options: Ring strain plus a partial positive charge
Epoxide carbons are always negatively charged
Oxygen in the ring is the electrophilic atom, not carbon
Epoxides have no dipole at all

electrophiles.q: Rank BF3, CH4, and CH3Cl in order of decreasing electrophilicity at their central/relevant carbon or boron atom.
Which has the more electrophilic carbonyl carbon, CH₃CHO or CF₃CHO?
options: CH₃CHO, because a methyl group is smaller than CF₃
CF₃CHO, because three fluorines pull density off the carbon
They are identical, since both of them are aldehydes
Neither of them, without an acid catalyst present

electrophiles.q: Adding an electron-withdrawing group (such as a second carbonyl or a halogen) near a carbonyl carbon generally makes that carbonyl carbon:
options: Less electrophilic, because electron-withdrawing groups donate electrons
More electrophilic, because more density is pulled away

electrophiles.q: A carbocation is generally considered one of the strongest electrophiles in organic chemistry because it has an empty orbital and carries a full positive charge.
Why is the carbon attached to a leaving group in an alkyl halide (e.g., the carbon in CH3–Br) considered electrophilic even though it is tetravalent and neutral?
options: The C–Br bond is polarized, leaving carbon δ+
The hydrogens on that carbon make it electrophilic
Bromine is more electron-poor than carbon
Alkyl halides are not electrophilic at all

electrophiles.q: Which halogen-containing species acts as the electrophile when Br2 reacts with an alkene in a bromination addition reaction?
options: The alkene is the electrophile in this reaction
Br2, polarized by the approaching alkene

electrophiles.q: A Lewis acid such as AlCl3 is classified as an electrophile because it:
options: Has a complete octet and no room to accept electrons
Has an empty orbital to accept an electron pair

electrophiles.q: Protonation of an alcohol by a strong acid converts the alcohol's oxygen region into a better leaving group, but does this make the adjacent carbon a better or worse electrophile?
options: Worse electrophile, because protonation adds more electron density
No change in electrophilicity at all
The carbon becomes a nucleophile instead
Better electrophile, since the positive oxygen withdraws more

electrophiles.q: Which of the following carbonyl-containing compounds has the most electrophilic carbonyl carbon, making it the most reactive toward nucleophiles?
A carboxylate ion (RCOO-) is generally a poor electrophile at its carbonyl carbon.
Why can a simple, unactivated alkane like ethane not act as an electrophile under ordinary conditions?
options: It has too many electrons overall
No polar bonds and no empty orbital
Alkanes react instantly with every nucleophile

electrophiles.q: In an SN1 mechanism, which species formed as an intermediate is the actual electrophile attacked by the incoming nucleophile?
options: The original alkyl halide before ionization
The leaving group itself after it departs
The carbocation intermediate formed after the leaving group departs

electrophiles.q: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is generally more electrophilic than a ketone's carbonyl carbon because:
options: Aldehydes have an extra electron-withdrawing oxygen
Ketones have no carbonyl carbon at all
Aldehydes have one fewer donating alkyl group

electrophiles.q: An aromatic ring undergoing electrophilic aromatic substitution reacts with an electrophile such as Br+ generated from Br2 and a Lewis acid catalyst.
Which statement correctly relates electrophile strength to reaction rate with a given nucleophile?
options: Stronger electrophiles (more electron-poor, more accessible) generally react faster with a given nucleophile, all else equal
Stronger electrophiles generally react more slowly because they are more stable
Electrophile strength has no bearing on reaction rate
Only nucleophile strength affects reaction rate, never electrophile strength

electrophiles.q: In a protonated ketone the plus sign is drawn on oxygen. Which atom does a nucleophile attack?
options: The oxygen, because that is where the charge is drawn
The carbon, because that is the atom short of density
Neither, since a protonated ketone resists nucleophiles
Whichever of the two the nucleophile reaches first

electrophiles.q: Why does conjugation of a carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond (as in an enone, an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone) create a second electrophilic site at the beta carbon?
options: Conjugation has no effect on electrophilicity anywhere in the molecule
The beta carbon becomes negatively charged instead
Resonance places partial positive charge on the beta carbon
Only the carbonyl carbon is ever electrophilic in an enone

electrophiles.q: Which of the following best explains why CO2 (carbon dioxide) reacts readily as an electrophile with strong nucleophiles like Grignard reagents?
options: CO2's oxygen atoms are the electrophilic sites, not carbon
CO2 cannot react with any nucleophile
Two oxygens leave its carbon very electron-poor

electrophiles.q: Why does protonating a ketone's oxygen make its carbon a far better electrophile?
options: The proton attaches to the carbon and gives it a positive charge
A contributor now places a full positive charge on that carbon
The carbonyl pi bond is destroyed outright by the incoming proton
Protonation turns the oxygen itself into the site of attack

electrophiles.q: A terminal alkyne's acidic proton can be removed by a strong base. In this acid-base reaction, which species is acting as the electrophile?
options: The acidic hydrogen atom on the terminal alkyne carbon

electrophiles.q: What makes sulfonate esters (like tosylates, R-OTs) useful electrophiles in substitution reactions, much like alkyl halides?
options: Sulfonates make carbon into a nucleophile
Sulfonate esters have no leaving group at all
Sulfur is the site that nucleophiles attack, not carbon

electrophiles.q: In general, increasing the number of electron-donating alkyl substituents directly on an electrophilic carbon tends to:
options: Increase its electrophilicity by adding more positive character
Have absolutely no effect on electrophilicity under any circumstances
Decrease its electrophilicity by donating density and bulk
Convert the carbon into a full nucleophile

electrophiles.q: A tertiary carbocation forms more readily than a primary carbocation.
Which best explains why methyl iodide (CH3I) is often used as a model electrophile in SN2 reactions despite iodine being a relatively weak inductive electron-withdrawer compared to fluorine?
options: Iodine makes the carbon extremely electron-rich
Methyl iodide has no electrophilic carbon
Fluorine is always a better leaving group than iodine
Iodide is an excellent, polarizable leaving group

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group is generally one that is:
options: Stable once it departs with the electron pair (weak base)
Unable to hold a negative charge

leaving-groups.q: Which of these is typically the best leaving group?
An alcohol does not react with NaBr, but the same alcohol with HBr gives the alkyl bromide. What does the acid change?
options: It makes bromide a stronger nucleophile than it was before
It protonates the OH, so the group that leaves is water
It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
It adds positive charge directly onto the reacting carbon

leaving-groups.q: A good leaving group should be the conjugate base of a:
Methylamine derivatives will not do substitution at the C–N bond, but a quaternary ammonium salt R–N(CH₃)₃⁺ will. What has changed?
options: The three methyl groups make the neighboring carbon markedly more electron-poor
A positively charged nitrogen is more electronegative and holds the pair better
The group now departs as a neutral trialkylamine instead of as an amide anion
The C–N bond is longer in the salt and therefore easier to break homolytically

leaving-groups.q: Rank Cl-, Br-, and I- in order of decreasing ability to act as a leaving group.
options: All three are identical leaving groups

leaving-groups.q: Why is F- generally a poor leaving group compared to the other halides even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen?
options: Fluorine cannot form a stable anion
Fluoride is a strong base and holds its charge tightly
The C–F bond is the weakest of all the C–halogen bonds
Fluoride is actually the best leaving group of the halides

leaving-groups.q: A tosylate group (OTs-, the conjugate base of a strong sulfonic acid) is considered an excellent leaving group for the same general reason that halides are, namely:
options: It is a strong base that holds electrons tightly
It has no negative charge when it leaves
It is a very weak, highly resonance-stabilized base that readily accommodates the departing negative charge
It forms only under basic conditions

leaving-groups.q: Amide ion (NH2-) is generally considered one of the worst common leaving groups in organic chemistry.
Why does protonating the oxygen of an alcohol (forming R-OH2+) convert a poor leaving group into a good one?
options: Protonation removes the leaving group entirely
Protonation has no effect on leaving group ability
Protonation makes oxygen a better nucleophile instead
Protonation gives neutral water, a weak base

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following is generally NOT a good leaving group under typical SN1/SN2 conditions?
Resonance stabilization of the departing anion (as in a sulfonate or carboxylate leaving group) generally makes that group a better leaving group.
In the reaction of an epoxide with a nucleophile under basic conditions, what effectively serves as the leaving group when the ring opens?
options: The ring oxygen, which becomes an alkoxide as the strained C–O bond breaks

leaving-groups.q: Why is it generally true that weaker bases make better leaving groups?
options: Weak bases are more electronegative than strong bases in every case
Weak bases always carry a positive charge
A weak base holds negative charge comfortably, so it departs readily
There is no real relationship between base strength and leaving group ability

leaving-groups.q: Which species would you predict to be a better leaving group: the conjugate base of acetic acid (CH3COO-, pKa of acid ≈ 4.8) or the conjugate base of ethanol (CH3CH2O-, pKa of acid ≈ 16)?
options: Ethoxide, because alcohols are weaker acids
They are equally good leaving groups
Neither can ever act as a leaving group
Acetate, because it is the conjugate base of the stronger acid and is therefore a weaker, more stable base

leaving-groups.q: A carbocation can be thought of as having 'lost' a leaving group from the original substrate. Which best describes the leaving group's role right before departure?
options: It must be stable once it takes the electron pair
It must remain a strong nucleophile even as it departs
It must become more reactive after leaving
It plays no role in determining the reaction rate

leaving-groups.q: Converting an alcohol's -OH into a mesylate (OMs) or tosylate (OTs) group before a substitution reaction is a common strategy because:
options: It makes the oxygen a stronger base
It turns a poor leaving group into a sulfonate
Mesylates and tosylates are never good leaving groups
It removes the need for any leaving group at all

leaving-groups.q: A proposed mechanism has a nucleophile attacking a carbon while hydroxide is pushed off that same carbon. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong; this is an ordinary substitution step
Hydroxide is a strong base and will not leave unassisted
The nucleophile ought to attack the oxygen instead
Two arrows may not be drawn within one mechanism step

leaving-groups.q: Which leaving group would most likely make an SN2 reaction proceed fastest, all else being equal: Cl-, Br-, or a tosylate (OTs-)?
options: Cl-, because it is the smallest
Br-, because halides are always best
Tosylate, a very weak, stable base
All three give identical reaction rates

leaving-groups.q: An amine (R–NH₂) is a poor leaving group, but it can depart once its nitrogen carries a positive charge, as in R–NH₃⁺ or R–NR₃⁺, because what leaves is then a neutral amine.
Why does pKa of the leaving group's conjugate acid serve as a useful predictor of leaving group ability?
options: Higher pKa always means a better leaving group
pKa has no relationship to leaving group ability
pKa only matters for nucleophiles, not leaving groups
Lower pKa means a weaker, more stable base

leaving-groups.q: Which of these would you predict to be the best leaving group based on its conjugate acid's strength: leaving group X whose conjugate acid has pKa 9, or leaving group Y whose conjugate acid has pKa -7?
options: Leaving group Y, the much weaker and more stable base
Leaving group X, because higher pKa means a better leaving group
Both are equally good leaving groups regardless of pKa
pKa values cannot be used to compare leaving groups

leaving-groups.q: Cyanide ion (CN-) is generally a poor leaving group.
In a Grignard or organolithium reagent, the carbon bonded to the metal behaves as a strong nucleophile/base. If this carbon were instead asked to act as a leaving group, what would you predict?
options: It would be an excellent leaving group, since strong bases always make excellent leaving groups too
It would be an extremely poor leaving group, since strong bases resist departing
Leaving group ability is unrelated to nucleophilicity or basicity in this case
Carbanions cannot be discussed in terms of leaving group ability at all

leaving-groups.q: Which best explains why water (H2O) can act as a leaving group in acid-catalyzed reactions but hydroxide (OH-) generally cannot under the same mild acidic conditions?
options: Water and hydroxide are equally good leaving groups always
Hydroxide has no electron pairs to take with it
Water is a weak base; hydroxide is a much stronger one
Water cannot leave under any circumstances

leaving-groups.q: A substitution refuses to run, even with a large excess of an excellent nucleophile and a long reaction time. Which change is most likely to make it go?
options: Add more of the same nucleophile, since rate rises with its concentration
Convert the leaving group into one whose anion is a much weaker base
Lower the temperature so the starting material is not destroyed
Switch to a less polar solvent so the reagents are more concentrated

leaving-groups.q: Phosphate groups (such as those in ATP) are biologically important leaving groups. Why are they effective leaving groups despite carrying a full negative charge?
options: Phosphate has no resonance stabilization at all
Phosphate groups are actually poor leaving groups in every biological context
Phosphate always leaves as a neutral, uncharged species
Its charge is delocalized over several oxygens by resonance

leaving-groups.q: Which of the following best ranks typical leaving group ability from best to worst: I-, OH-, OTs-?
A trifluoromethanesulfonate group (triflate, OTf-) is considered one of the best leaving groups known, even better than tosylate, largely because of the strongly electron-withdrawing fluorines.
If a leaving group is a poor one (a strong base) in a proposed SN1 mechanism, what is the most likely consequence for the reaction?
options: The reaction proceeds at the same rate regardless of leaving group quality
Ionization becomes rate-limiting and the reaction is very slow
The reaction mechanism switches automatically to E2

energy-diagrams.q: On a reaction-coordinate diagram, what is plotted on the vertical axis?
The activation energy of a step is measured from which two points?
options: From the species in front of the hill up to the peak
From the lowest point on the whole diagram up to the peak
From the peak down to the products
From the reactants across to the products

energy-diagrams.q: A reaction is described as exergonic. What does that tell you about the diagram?
options: The product plateau lies below the reactant plateau
The product plateau lies above the reactant plateau
There is more than one hump

energy-diagrams.q: A maximum on a reaction-coordinate diagram corresponds to what?
A shallow well sitting between two humps on an energy diagram represents what?
options: The activated complex at the top of the barrier
The activation energy of the second step

energy-diagrams.q: A mechanism's energy diagram shows three humps. How many steps and intermediates does the mechanism have?
Which quantity determines how fast a reaction proceeds?
options: The overall free-energy change of the reaction
The activation energy of the rate-determining step
The equilibrium constant for the reaction
The energy of the product relative to the intermediate

energy-diagrams.q: Why is a transition state impossible to isolate and put in a bottle?
options: It is too reactive toward oxygen to survive handling
It carries a charge that neutralizes on contact with glass
It exists in too low a concentration to weigh out
It is an energy maximum with partly formed bonds, not a species sitting in a well

energy-diagrams.q: What does adding a catalyst do to a reaction-coordinate diagram?
options: Lowers the peak while leaving both plateaus where they were
Lowers the product plateau so the reaction becomes more downhill
Raises the reactant plateau so less climbing is needed
Removes the transition state from the pathway

energy-diagrams.q: The horizontal axis of a reaction-coordinate diagram measures what?
options: The time elapsed during the reaction
The temperature of the reaction mixture
How far the structural change from reactants to products has progressed
The molar amount of reactant consumed

energy-diagrams.q: Reaction A: activation energy 35 kcal/mol, overall change −40 kcal/mol. Reaction B: activation energy 14 kcal/mol, overall change −1 kcal/mol. Which is faster at room temperature?
options: Reaction A, from its much larger release of energy
Reaction B, from its much smaller barrier
Both proceed at the same rate
The comparison needs the equilibrium constants

energy-diagrams.q: A two-step mechanism has TS1 at +20 kcal/mol above the reactants, an intermediate at +12, and TS2 at +24. Which step is rate-determining?
options: Step 2, whose transition state is the highest point drawn
Step 2, being the step that delivers the product
Step 1, whose climb of 20 exceeds step 2's climb of 12

energy-diagrams.q: An equilibrium lies 90:10 in favor of product. A catalyst is added and the mixture is left to equilibrate again. What is the new ratio?
options: Closer to 50:50, from the faster reverse reaction
Better than 90:10, from the lower barrier
Impossible to say without the activation energy

energy-diagrams.q: Warming a reaction from 25 °C to 35 °C roughly doubles its rate. What is the best explanation?
options: The activation energy falls as temperature rises
The products become more stable at the higher temperature
A larger fraction of molecules now carries enough energy to clear the barrier

energy-diagrams.q: Reaction X has an overall free-energy change of −1.4 kcal/mol and reaction Y one of −4.2 kcal/mol at 25 °C. Roughly how do their equilibrium constants compare?
options: Y's K is about three times X's
Y's K is about one hundred times X's
The two constants are about equal
X's K is the larger of the two

energy-diagrams.q: According to the Hammond postulate, what does the transition state of a strongly exothermic step resemble?
options: The reactants, with bonds barely changed
The products, with the new bonds essentially complete
A structure exactly midway between the two
The most stable intermediate available on the pathway

energy-diagrams.q: Two competing pathways, each a single irreversible step, lead to products of different stability. In which case will the product ratio most strongly favor the more stable product?
options: When the product-forming step is endothermic
When the product-forming step is strongly exothermic
When both pathways share the same intermediate
When the reaction is run at higher temperature

energy-diagrams.q: A first step has a 22 kcal/mol barrier and the second step a 4 kcal/mol barrier. A change to the substrate cuts the second barrier to 2 kcal/mol. What happens to the overall rate?
options: It rises by about a factor of ten
It falls, from the deeper well before the second step

energy-diagrams.q: Lowering a reaction's activation energy by about 2.8 kcal/mol at 25 °C multiplies the rate by roughly what factor?
A one-step reaction has a forward activation energy of 20 kcal/mol and an overall change of −8 kcal/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
Which species would correctly be drawn inside square brackets with a double dagger?
options: A carbocation with a full positive charge and three complete bonds
A carbon with a partly broken bond to the leaving group drawn dotted
A radical with an unpaired electron shown as a dot
A protonated alcohol carrying a positive oxygen

energy-diagrams.q: A student argues that a reaction releasing 50 kcal/mol must be fast. What is wrong with the reasoning?
options: The energy released is measured in the wrong units for a rate
A large release of energy raises the barrier in proportion
The released energy describes the plateau gap, and the rate depends on the barrier
Energy released is unrelated to the position of the equilibrium

energy-diagrams.q: An endothermic step is said to have a late transition state. What does 'late' mean here?
options: It happens later in time than the other steps
The peak occurs far along the reaction coordinate, close to the products
The peak is higher than any other on the diagram
The step is preceded by a deep well

energy-diagrams.q: Hydrogen abstraction by chlorine is exothermic while the same abstraction by bromine is endothermic. Which reagent distinguishes a tertiary hydrogen from a primary one more sharply?
options: Bromine, whose late transition state already contains the radical
Chlorine, whose greater reactivity lets it choose the weakest bond
Both distinguish them equally, since the radical stabilities are the same
Neither shows measurable selectivity between the two

energy-diagrams.q: Which statement about a catalyst and the reverse reaction is correct?
options: It speeds the forward direction and slows the reverse
It affects the reverse direction not at all
It lowers the reverse barrier by the same amount as the forward barrier
It converts an endergonic reaction into an exergonic one

energy-diagrams.q: Relative to the reactants: TS1 sits at +14, the intermediate at +2, TS2 at +18 kcal/mol. Which step is rate-determining, and what is its barrier?
Ionization of an alkyl halide to a carbocation and a halide ion is endothermic. Using the Hammond postulate, what follows about the rate of that step?
options: The rate is governed by the strength of the carbon–halogen bond alone
All alkyl halides ionize at comparable rates, the transition state being reactant-like
The rate tracks the stability of the carbocation closely, the transition state being cation-like
The rate depends on the stability of the starting halide rather than the cation

energy-diagrams.q: A one-step reaction has a forward barrier of 15 kcal/mol and an overall change of +6 kcal/mol. Which statement about it is correct?
options: The reverse barrier is 9 kcal/mol, so the reverse direction is faster
The reverse barrier is 21 kcal/mol, so the forward direction is faster
Both barriers are 15 kcal/mol, so the two rates match
The reverse barrier is 6 kcal/mol, so equilibrium favors the reactants

energy-diagrams.q: Two products can form from one intermediate. The route to P1 has the lower barrier; P2 sits in the deeper well. The reaction is run cold under conditions where neither product can revert. What is obtained?
options: Mainly P2, the more stable of the two
Mainly P1, whose barrier is lower
A 50:50 mixture, the intermediate being common to both
No reaction at all under cold conditions

energy-diagrams.q: An uncatalyzed reaction has a forward barrier of 25 kcal/mol and an overall change of −10 kcal/mol. A catalyst cuts the forward barrier to 18 kcal/mol. What is the reverse barrier with the catalyst present?

carbocations.q: A carbocation carbon is best described as:
options: sp³, tetrahedral, with a lone pair in the fourth orbital
sp², trigonal planar, with an empty p orbital perpendicular to the plane
sp, linear, with two empty p orbitals
sp², trigonal planar, with a lone pair above the plane

carbocations.q: How many valence electrons surround the positively charged carbon of a carbocation?
A carbon is drawn with three bonds and no lone pair. Its formal charge is:
Rank these cations from most to least stable: (CH₃)₃C⁺, CH₃CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₂CH⁺, CH₃⁺.
options: They are all about equally stable

carbocations.q: What is the name for a sigma bond donating its electron pair into an adjacent empty p orbital?
Which is the direct precursor event for most carbocations you will draw?
options: A leaving group departs, taking the bonding pair with it
A radical abstracts a hydrogen atom
Two carbons share an electron pair equally

carbocations.q: Which pair of cations is closest in stability?
options: A primary alkyl cation and a benzylic cation
A primary benzylic cation and a tertiary alkyl cation
A methyl cation and a tertiary alkyl cation
A vinyl cation and a secondary alkyl cation

carbocations.q: What migrates during a 1,2-hydride shift?
options: A bare proton, leaving the electrons behind
A hydrogen atom with one electron
A hydride ion arriving from the solvent
A hydrogen together with the two electrons of its bond

carbocations.q: In a carbocation, the empty p orbital is exposed:
options: Only on the face the leaving group came from
Only on the face opposite the leaving group
Along the plane of the three bonds
Equally on both faces of the trigonal plane

carbocations.q: Which statement about induction as a stabilizing effect is correct?
options: Induction moves the charge fully onto the neighboring carbon
An alkyl group donates electron density along the sigma bond because it is more polarizable than a hydrogen
An alkyl group withdraws electron density, which spreads the charge
Induction requires the neighboring bond to align with the empty p orbital

carbocations.q: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and 1-chlorobutane are each warmed in aqueous ethanol. Which ionizes faster, and why?
options: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, because it gives a tertiary cation
1-chlorobutane, because its carbon is less crowded so the bond breaks more easily
1-chlorobutane, because a primary C–Cl bond is weaker
Neither — ionization rate does not depend on substitution

carbocations.q: Which cation in this list is the most stable?
Why does the π system of a benzene ring fail to stabilize a positive charge on one of its own ring carbons?
options: A benzene ring is electron-poor and has no density to donate
The empty orbital is an sp² hybrid lying in the ring plane, at 90° to the π cloud
The ring's π electrons are already committed to aromaticity and cannot be shared
The ring carbon rehybridizes to sp³, which destroys the conjugation

carbocations.q: A student draws the tert-butyl cation with a lone pair on the central carbon. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing — the lone pair is how the positive charge is shown
The lone pair belongs on one of the methyl carbons instead
The central carbon should be drawn sp³
That structure is a carbanion with a formal charge of −1, not a cation

carbocations.q: The cation shown has no hydrogen on the carbon adjacent to the charge. What is its fate?
options: A hydrogen migrates from two carbons away, giving a secondary cation
It loses a proton to give an alkene without rearranging
A methyl migrates from the quaternary carbon, giving a tertiary cation
It cannot rearrange, so it is captured as the primary cation

carbocations.q: Where does the tail of the curved arrow go when drawing a 1,2-methyl shift?
options: On the bond between the migrating methyl and the carbon it is leaving
On the positively charged carbon, pointing at the methyl
On one of the methyl's C–H bonds
On the lone pair of the cationic carbon

carbocations.q: An alkene is protonated. Which carbon ends up bearing the positive charge?
options: The one that gives the more stable cation, which is usually the more substituted carbon
The one that already carries more hydrogens
Whichever carbon the proton adds to
The less substituted carbon, because it is less crowded

carbocations.q: Why is a vinyl cation, with the positive charge on a doubly bonded carbon, so unstable?
options: The double bond withdraws electron density inductively from every nearby atom
It has eight electrons and so cannot accept any more
It is linear and sp-hybridized, and its empty p orbital is perpendicular to the adjacent π bond
Its empty orbital is fully conjugated with the π bond, which destabilizes both

carbocations.q: Cations A and B differ only in that a shift converting A to B would leave the charge on a carbon with the same substitution. What happens?
options: The shift happens anyway, because cations always rearrange
Both shift back and forth until one is consumed, giving equal products
A rearranges twice to reach a tertiary cation
No shift is favored, because there is no gain in stability

carbocations.q: Which observation is the clearest evidence that a reaction passes through a free carbocation?
options: The reaction is faster in a polar aprotic solvent
The product's carbon skeleton differs from the starting material's
The rate doubles when the nucleophile concentration doubles
The product is a single inverted enantiomer

carbocations.q: Why does a more stable carbocation also form faster?
options: The more stable cation has a lower activation energy for the second step
Stability and rate are unrelated; the correlation is coincidental
The step is endothermic, so its transition state comes late and resembles the cation
Stable species always form faster than unstable ones, as a general law

carbocations.q: Which cation is the least stable of these four?
An oxygen directly attached to a cationic carbon stabilizes it strongly, even though oxygen is highly electronegative. Why?
options: It hydrogen-bonds to the solvent, stabilizing the ion
Its lone pair forms a π bond to the carbon, giving a structure with an octet on every atom
It withdraws electron density inductively, which spreads the positive charge
Its size lets it disperse the charge over a large volume

carbocations.q: Which substrate would you expect NOT to ionize to a carbocation under solvolysis conditions?
Which factor decides whether a hydrogen on a neighboring carbon will migrate to a cation?
options: How many hydrogens that neighboring carbon carries
How close the hydrogen is to the leaving group that departed
Whether the hydrogen is on a primary or secondary carbon originally
What cation the migration would leave behind

carbocations.q: The compound shown solvolyzes in water to give mainly cyclopentanol rather than cyclobutylmethanol. What accounts for the five-membered ring?
options: Chloride leaves from a ring carbon rather than from the exocyclic carbon
A ring C–C bond migrates to the exocyclic carbon, expanding the ring and leaving a secondary cation
A hydride shifts from the ring, giving a secondary cyclobutyl cation that then opens
Water attacks the ring directly, breaking one of its C–C bonds

carbocations.q: The alcohol shown is treated with HBr. What is the major product?
A textbook draws a primary substrate ionizing to a free primary cation, which then rearranges. What is the honest correction to that picture?
options: The rearrangement happens after the nucleophile attacks, not before
The primary cation forms but is captured before it can shift
The migration begins as the leaving group departs, so the two events are really one step
Primary substrates never react at all, so the mechanism is entirely wrong

carbocations.q: Ionizing the compound shown gives a single cation, yet two different alcohols come out of the flask. What explains this without invoking any 1,2-shift?
options: The double bond migrates by a separate acid-catalyzed step after the product forms
The cation is an allylic hybrid, so the nucleophile can attack at either end of the delocalized system
A hydride shifts along the chain before water attacks
Two different cations form at comparable rates from the same substrate

carbocations.q: Compare a tertiary alkyl cation with a secondary cation that has an adjacent oxygen bearing a lone pair. Which is more stable, and what does that imply for a substrate carrying both features elsewhere in the molecule?
options: The tertiary one, because alkyl substitution always outranks a heteroatom
They are equal, so a mixture of both cations forms
Neither forms, because the oxygen deactivates the whole molecule
The oxygen-stabilized one, so ionization occurs next to the oxygen even if a more substituted carbon is available

electron-rich-poor.q: An electron-rich atom in a mechanism tends to act as a(n):
Why is the carbon of C=O electron-poor while the oxygen is electron-rich?
options: There is no difference — they’re equal

electron-rich-poor.q: In a C–Mg bond (as in a Grignard reagent), which atom is electron-rich?

options: Aldehydes and ketones have essentially zero dipole moment, identical to alkanes
The C=O bond gives aldehydes and ketones a significant permanent dipole moment, higher than comparable alkanes
Only aromatic ketones have a measurable dipole moment
Dipole moment is irrelevant to boiling point

aldehydes-ketones.q: A student says the carbonyl OXYGEN must be the electrophile because it is the atom carrying a charge. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing; the oxygen is attacked by nucleophiles
The oxygen carries a partial positive charge, not a negative one
The charge is negative, so oxygen is the basic site and carbon is attacked
Neither atom is charged, so the molecule has no electrophilic site at all

aldehydes-ketones.q: A chemist needs a quick bench test that gives a visible result with an aldehyde and no result with a ketone. Which reagent does that?
Which of the following best explains why steric bulk around the carbonyl carbon reduces reactivity toward nucleophilic addition in ketones compared to aldehydes?
options: Bulkier groups increase the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Bulkier groups make the carbonyl oxygen more basic, which has no effect on sterics
Steric bulk has no measurable effect on reaction rate
Bulky groups hinder the nucleophile's approach, raising the barrier

aldehydes-ketones.q: Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is less electrophilic than that of a comparable aliphatic aldehyde mainly because of:
options: Resonance donation from the ring into the carbonyl
Steric hindrance from the phenyl ring blocking nucleophiles
The phenyl ring's inductive electron withdrawal, which increases electrophilicity
Hydrogen bonding between the ring and the carbonyl oxygen

aldehydes-ketones.q: A molecule containing both an aldehyde group and a ketone group in the same chain would be named using which suffix for the principal characteristic group?
options: Both suffixes are used together as '-alone'
Neither; it must be renamed as a diketone

aldehydes-ketones.q: Glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone are both three-carbon sugars that differ specifically in that one is an aldehyde and the other is a ketone.

nucleophilic-addition.q: In nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, the nucleophile attacks:
What happens to the C=O pi bond during nucleophilic addition?
options: It breaks, pushing electrons onto the oxygen as an alkoxide
It becomes a new sigma bond to the nucleophile without changing oxygen

nucleophilic-addition.q: After a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl, what intermediate typically forms before a final proton transfer?
In the mechanism of base-catalyzed nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, what is generally the rate-determining step?
options: Attack of the nucleophile on the carbonyl carbon

nucleophilic-addition.q: Under acid catalysis, the carbonyl oxygen is typically protonated before the nucleophile attacks.
A synthesis calls for CH3MgBr to be added to a molecule that contains a ketone and, elsewhere, a free OH group. What happens?
options: The Grignard adds to the ketone and ignores the OH
The Grignard is destroyed by the OH proton before it can add
The OH group adds to the ketone in an intramolecular reaction
The Grignard reduces the OH to a C-H bond

nucleophilic-addition.q: When cyanide ion (CN-) adds to an aldehyde, the product formed (before any workup) is called a:
When a primary amine adds to a ketone and the reaction proceeds to completion with loss of water, the final product is typically a(n):
A secondary amine reacting with a ketone that has an alpha hydrogen ultimately forms an enamine rather than an imine, because:
options: Secondary amines cannot form a hemiaminal intermediate at all
Enamines are less stable than imines and therefore always form first
Secondary amines are stronger nucleophiles than primary amines
The nitrogen has no H left to lose, so an alpha C-H is lost

nucleophilic-addition.q: Grignard reagents (RMgX) add to aldehydes and ketones via nucleophilic addition, and the resulting alkoxide must be protonated in a separate aqueous acid workup step to give the final alcohol.
Why is addition of a Grignard reagent to a carbonyl considered essentially irreversible, unlike addition of water or an alcohol?
options: Because both the alkoxide and the carbanion are poor leaving groups
Because the carbon-carbon bond formed is extremely weak and can easily break
Because Grignard reagents do not actually bond to the carbonyl carbon
Because the reaction only occurs in the gas phase

nucleophilic-addition.q: An ester treated with excess CH3MgBr gives a tertiary alcohol carrying two new methyl groups, not a ketone. Why can the reaction not be stopped at the ketone?
options: The ketone intermediate is more electrophilic than the ester was
Esters cannot form a tetrahedral intermediate at all
The second methyl group adds to the ester oxygen rather than the carbon
Grignard reagents add twice to every carbonyl, including ketones

nucleophilic-addition.q: Compared to hydroxide ion, water is a much weaker nucleophile toward carbonyls mainly because:
options: Water has no lone pairs on oxygen
Hydroxide's charge makes its lone pairs more available
Water is a larger molecule than hydroxide
Water cannot approach the carbonyl carbon at the correct angle

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which factor would be expected to INCREASE the electrophilicity of a carbonyl carbon, making it more reactive toward nucleophilic addition?
options: Placing an electron-donating alkyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon
Increasing steric bulk around the carbonyl carbon
Placing an electron-withdrawing group (such as a halogen) near the carbonyl carbon
Conjugating the carbonyl with an aromatic ring

nucleophilic-addition.q: The aldehyde shown is significantly MORE reactive toward nucleophilic addition than acetaldehyde. The best explanation is:
options: The three chlorine atoms sterically shield the carbonyl, slowing addition
Chlorine atoms donate electrons into the carbonyl through resonance
Chlorine has no electronic effect on nearby carbons
The three chlorines withdraw electron density inductively

nucleophilic-addition.q: In nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, what structural change happens to the carbonyl carbon's hybridization and geometry?
options: It stays sp2 and trigonal planar throughout
It changes from sp3 to sp2
It becomes sp hybridized and linear

nucleophilic-addition.q: During nucleophilic addition, the two pi electrons of the C=O bond end up localized as a lone pair on the oxygen atom.
Which nucleophile, added to a ketone in a single equivalent, gives a product whose carbon carries both an OH and an OR group?
If a nucleophile adds to one face of a planar carbonyl carbon and creates a new stereocenter, with no other chiral influence present, the product forms as:
Ketones generally undergo nucleophilic addition more slowly than aldehydes for what combination of reasons?
options: Only steric effects matter; electronics are identical
Only electronic effects matter; sterics are identical
Ketones simply lack a carbonyl carbon
More steric hindrance and less electrophilicity

nucleophilic-addition.q: Nucleophilic ADDITION to an aldehyde/ketone and nucleophilic ACYL SUBSTITUTION at a carboxylic acid derivative (like an ester) both proceed through a tetrahedral intermediate, but they differ because:
options: Only acyl substitution expels a leaving group
Addition has no tetrahedral intermediate at all
Acyl substitution never involves a nucleophile
Aldehydes and ketones always have a leaving group attached

nucleophilic-addition.q: Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) delivering a hydride ion to a ketone's carbonyl carbon is an example of nucleophilic addition in which hydride acts as the nucleophile.
Which of the following is the best order of relative nucleophile strength toward a carbonyl carbon, from STRONGEST to WEAKEST, for this set: hydride (from LiAlH4), an amine, and water?
options: All three are equally nucleophilic toward carbonyls

nucleophilic-addition.q: A strong, weakly basic nucleophile such as iodide ion (I-) reacts poorly with aldehydes and ketones in simple nucleophilic addition reactions. Why?
options: Iodide has no lone pairs available
Iodide's negative charge repels the carbonyl oxygen, preventing any approach
Iodide is weakly basic and an excellent leaving group
Carbonyls never react with halide ions for any reason

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes how an acid catalyst versus a base catalyst helps nucleophilic addition of an alcohol to a ketone proceed?
options: Acid and base catalysis work by an identical mechanism with no meaningful difference
Base protonates the carbonyl oxygen; acid deprotonates the alcohol
Neither acid nor base has any effect on this reaction
Acid protonates the carbonyl; base deprotonates the alcohol

nucleophilic-addition.q: You need the alcohol shown. Which carbonyl and organometallic pair would you use?
Which best describes why an alkoxide intermediate formed during nucleophilic addition is typically quenched with water or dilute acid at the end of a reaction?
options: To protonate the alkoxide to the neutral alcohol
To oxidize the alkoxide into a carboxylic acid
To reverse the addition and regenerate starting carbonyl

nucleophilic-addition.q: When comparing nucleophilic addition rates, an aldehyde reacting with a bulky nucleophile (such as a branched Grignard reagent) will generally react slower than with a small nucleophile (such as methylmagnesium bromide), due to:
options: Electronic effects dominating entirely, with no steric component
Steric hindrance in the tetrahedral transition state
Bulky nucleophiles always being poor nucleophiles electronically
No difference; nucleophile size never matters

nucleophilic-addition.q: During acid-catalyzed addition of an alcohol to a ketone, protonating the carbonyl oxygen converts the neutral ketone into a resonance-stabilized cation often described as an oxocarbenium-like species before nucleophilic attack occurs.

If two different carbonyl compounds are placed in a flask along with a limited amount of a moderately strong nucleophile, which one would you expect to react fastest: an unhindered aliphatic aldehyde, or a sterically hindered diaryl ketone?
options: The diaryl ketone, because aromatic stabilization speeds up addition
They would react at identical rates
The aldehyde, less hindered and more electrophilic
Neither would react under any circumstances

acetals.q: An acetal forms from a carbonyl reacting with how many equivalents of alcohol (under acid catalysis)?
options: Two, giving a full acetal (two ether-like oxygens)

acetals.q: Acetals are stable under basic conditions but revert back to the carbonyl under:
Why are acetals useful as protecting groups for aldehydes/ketones during multi-step synthesis?
options: They make the carbonyl more reactive, not less
They resist base yet hydrolyze in acid
They only work on carboxylic acids

acetals.q: Acetal formation has just reached the oxocarbenium ion. What is the next step?
options: A hydride shifts to the positive carbon
The oxocarbenium loses a proton to give an alkene
A second alcohol attacks the oxocarbenium carbon

acetals.q: A hemiacetal carbon bears both an -OH group and an -OR group attached to the same carbon, along with an H and/or R group from the original carbonyl.
You need to protect a ketone as a SIX-membered cyclic acetal. Which diol does that?
A molecule contains a ketone, a tert-butyl ether and a tertiary alcohol. Is an acetal a safe way to protect the ketone here?
options: Yes, because acetals are removed under basic conditions
Yes, because acetal formation and removal are both neutral
No, because the deprotection needs aqueous acid, which the rest of the molecule will not survive
No, because acetals cannot be made from ketones

acetals.q: Which term specifically describes an acetal made from a ketone (as opposed to an aldehyde)?
In the acid-catalyzed mechanism of acetal formation, after the first alcohol adds to give the protonated hemiacetal, what key intermediate forms upon loss of water?
options: An oxocarbenium ion (resonance-stabilized carbocation with an adjacent oxygen)

acetals.q: When a carbonyl compound reacts with a diol such as ethylene glycol under acid catalysis, the two hydroxyl groups can both attack the same carbonyl carbon, typically forming a:
options: A polymer with no defined ring size

acetals.q: Acetal formation from a carbonyl compound and an alcohol is an equilibrium reaction, and using a large excess of alcohol (or removing water as it forms, e.g., with a Dean-Stark trap) helps drive the equilibrium toward the acetal product.

Glucose in aqueous solution exists predominantly as a cyclic structure formed by an intramolecular reaction between its aldehyde carbon and one of its own hydroxyl groups. This cyclic form is best classified as a:
options: Ether with no other functional character

acetals.q: The anomeric carbon in a cyclic sugar hemiacetal is the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon before ring closure.
Open-chain hemiacetals are usually too unstable to isolate, yet glucose sits over 99% as its cyclic hemiacetal. What accounts for the difference?
options: The cyclic form is an acetal rather than a hemiacetal
Ring closure here is intramolecular and gives a five- or six-membered ring
Sugars are not in equilibrium with their open-chain form
The cyclic form has no OH group left to lose

acetals.q: Compared to ketones, aldehydes generally form acetals more readily under the same acid-catalyzed conditions. This is mainly due to:
options: Aldehydes having a more basic carbonyl oxygen
Ketones lacking a carbonyl group entirely
Acetal formation being impossible for ketones

acetals.q: A chemist performs a Grignard addition on a molecule containing both a ketone and an ester, wanting the Grignard reagent to react only with the ester. What is a reasonable strategy using acetal chemistry to achieve this selectivity?
options: Protect the ketone as a cyclic acetal, run the Grignard, then hydrolyze
There is no way to control this selectivity
Protect the ester as an acetal instead, since esters and acetals are chemically identical
Add excess water to deactivate the Grignard reagent near the ketone only

acetals.q: The compound shown holds both an aldehyde and a ketone. One equivalent of ethylene glycol with catalytic acid is added. Which carbonyl is protected?
options: The aldehyde, because it is the more reactive carbonyl
The ketone, because it is the more reactive carbonyl
Both equally, since acetal formation ignores substitution
Neither, because a diol needs two carbonyls to react

acetals.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical catalyst used to promote acetal formation from a ketone and an alcohol?
Once an acetal protecting group has been hydrolyzed under aqueous acid, the nucleophile that ultimately adds to regenerate the carbonyl (displacing the first leaving alcohol) is:
A hemiacetal is generally more stable (less likely to revert to starting materials) and easier to isolate than its corresponding fully-formed acetal.
The cyclic acetal shown is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid and heated. The expected outcome is:
options: The ring stays completely intact with no change
A new carbon-carbon bond forms across the ring
The ring is reduced to a cyclic ether with no oxygen lost
The acetal hydrolyzes, regenerating the original carbonyl compound and the free diol

acetals.q: Which statement correctly differentiates an acetal from an ether, even though both contain only C-O single bonds and no carbonyl?
options: An acetal carbon bears two oxygens, an ether carbon one
There is no real difference; they are the same functional group
An ether always contains a ring, while an acetal never does
Ethers react with Grignard reagents, but acetals never do

acetals.q: A route has to reduce an ester to a primary alcohol while leaving a ketone in the same molecule untouched. Which order of operations works?
options: Reduce with LiAlH4 first, then protect the ketone, then deprotect
Protect the ketone, reduce with LiAlH4, then hydrolyze the acetal
Reduce with NaBH4, which leaves both the ester and the ketone alone
Protect the ester as an acetal, then reduce with LiAlH4

acetals.q: During acetal formation, the overall reaction releases one equivalent of water as a byproduct for each acetal molecule formed from one carbonyl and two alcohol molecules.
Which best describes the overall transformation from carbonyl to acetal in terms of oxidation state of the central carbon?
options: The carbon is oxidized, since it gains more oxygen-containing bonds
The carbon is reduced to an alkane-like oxidation state
The oxidation state of that carbon stays essentially the same; acetal formation is an addition/substitution of oxygen-based groups, not a redox reaction
The transformation changes the carbon's hybridization but always involves electron transfer to a metal

acetals.q: In sugar chemistry, when a cyclic hemiacetal (like glucose's ring form) further reacts with a second alcohol under acid catalysis to 'lock in' a specific anomer, the product formed is called a:
options: Another hemiacetal, chemically identical to the starting material
A reducing sugar with enhanced reactivity
Glycoside (a full acetal of the sugar)

acetals.q: If excess water (rather than excess alcohol) is present in a reaction mixture containing an acetal and a catalytic amount of acid, the equilibrium position will generally favor:
options: Hydrolysis back to the carbonyl and alcohol
The acetal remaining fully intact indefinitely
Formation of an even more substituted acetal
No change, because water has no role in this equilibrium

acetals.q: An acetal can be formed intramolecularly when a single molecule contains both a carbonyl group and one or more hydroxyl groups positioned so that they can cyclize onto that carbonyl, as commonly seen in sugar chemistry.
A 1,3-dioxane ring (a six-membered cyclic acetal) is typically formed by protecting a ketone or aldehyde with which type of diol?
options: Ethylene glycol (a 1,2-diol), which gives a five-membered ring instead
1,3-propanediol (a 1,3-diol), whose two hydroxyls are spaced correctly to close a six-membered ring with the carbonyl carbon
Methanol, which is not a diol at all
Any monohydric alcohol works equally well

acetals.q: Compared to esters, acetals are generally much less susceptible to attack by basic nucleophiles like hydroxide or Grignard reagents.

oxidation-states.q: What is the working test for oxidation in organic chemistry?
options: Losing a whole electron from the atom
Gaining bonds to O or losing bonds to H

oxidation-states.q: Which of these transformations is a reduction at carbon?
Is hydrogenation of an alkene an oxidation or a reduction?
Adding HBr across an alkene is what, in redox terms?
options: Both an oxidation and a reduction

oxidation-states.q: Which of these compounds contains a carbon at oxidation state +3?
Acetaldehyde, CH3CHO, is oxidized to acetic acid, CH3CO2H. What happens to the oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon?
options: It stays at +3; only the O-H changes

oxidation-states.q: What is the oxidation state of carbon in methane?
What is the oxidation state of carbon in methanol?
What is the oxidation state of carbon in formaldehyde?
What is the oxidation state of the carboxyl carbon in acetic acid, CH3CO2H?
What is the oxidation state of carbon in CO2?
In methyl acetate, CH3-CO-O-CH3, what are the oxidation states of the carbonyl carbon and of the O-CH3 carbon?
Converting an alcohol to an alkyl halide is what kind of reaction?
A carboxylic acid, ester, amide and nitrile all have their key carbon at which oxidation state?
Why can a tertiary alcohol not be oxidized?
options: No C-H on the carbinol carbon

oxidation-states.q: How many times can a primary alcohol be oxidized?
How many times can a secondary alcohol be oxidized?
Ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, with Me2S workup gives acetone and acetaldehyde. What happens to the oxidation states of the two former alkene carbons?
options: Each rises by one: 0 to +1, and -1 to 0
Each rises by two: 0 to +2, and -1 to +1
One rises by two and the other falls by two
Neither changes, because a C=C simply becomes a C=O

oxidation-states.q: Hydroboration-oxidation turns propene, CH3CH=CH2, into propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH. What happens to the oxidation states of C1 and C2?
options: Both rise by one: oxygen was added, so it is an oxidation
Both fall by one: it is a reduction
C1 rises by two and C2 is unchanged
C1 rises by one and C2 falls by one, so overall it is neither

oxidation-states.q: Hydration of an alkene is what, in redox terms?
Which pair sits on the same rung of the ladder?
What does the ladder explain about acyl derivatives?
options: They interconvert by substitution, not redox
They are all equally reactive toward nucleophiles

oxidation-states.q: Ethyl acetate, CH3CO2CH2CH3, is reduced with LiAlH4. How far does the former carbonyl carbon move, and where does it end up?
options: Down two rungs, +3 to -1, as the CH2OH carbon of ethanol
Down one rung, +3 to +1, as the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde
Down three rungs, +3 to -3, as a CH3 carbon
Nowhere: swapping the ester oxygen is substitution

oxidation-states.q: Which conversion needs neither an oxidant nor a reductant?
Which of these transformations is NOT a redox change at carbon?
A synthesis has to turn CH3CH2CH2OH into CH3CH2CO2H. How many rungs is that, and what does it tell you about the reagent?
options: One rung up, so almost any oxidant will do
Two rungs down, so it needs a hydride reagent
No change in rung, so a nucleophile is enough
Two rungs up, so it needs an oxidant that does not stop at the aldehyde

oxidation-states.q: A Grignard adds to acetone. What happens to the oxidation state of the carbonyl carbon, and to the Grignard's carbon?
options: The carbonyl carbon falls by one and the Grignard carbon rises by one, so overall nothing is oxidized or reduced
Both carbons fall by one, so the reaction is a reduction
Neither carbon changes, because C-C bonds count zero
The carbonyl carbon rises by two, so the reaction is an oxidation

oxidation-states.q: Cyclohexene is treated with Br2 to give trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. In redox terms this is:
options: Neither, because two atoms add across the double bond
A reduction, because the pi bond is destroyed
An oxidation - two bonds to halogen gained, no C-H gained
Neither, because bromine is not oxygen

oxidation-states.q: Propene, CH3CH=CH2, is epoxidized with mCPBA. What happens to the oxidation states of the two former alkene carbons?
options: C1 rises by one and C2 falls by one, so it is neither
Neither changes, because the two carbons stay bonded
Each rises by one, a two-electron oxidation overall

oxidation-states.q: Getting from an ester down to an aldehyde requires what?

alcohol-oxidation.q: Hexan-1-ol is divided between two flasks. One gets PCC in CH2Cl2; the other gets Jones reagent. What does each flask contain afterwards?
An alcohol C4H10O turns Jones reagent from orange to green. The organic product is not acidic: it does not dissolve in aqueous NaHCO3. Which alcohol was it?
Cyclohexanol is treated with Jones reagent in acetone at 0 C. What is the product?
What does any of these reagents give from a tertiary alcohol?
Why does an aqueous chromium oxidation not stop at the aldehyde?
options: The reagent is simply far too strong
The aldehyde hydrates and is oxidized again

alcohol-oxidation.q: What is the key difference between PCC and Jones reagent?
Which reagent converts (E)-but-2-en-1-ol, CH3CH=CHCH2OH, into (E)-but-2-enal and leaves the C=C alone?
A molecule carries an allylic secondary alcohol and a saturated primary alcohol. Which reagent oxidizes only the allylic one?
3-Methylbutane-1,3-diol, HOCH2CH2C(CH3)2OH, is treated with excess Dess-Martin periodinane. What is the product?
options: No reaction: the tertiary OH blocks it
A keto-aldehyde, with both alcohols oxidized

alcohol-oxidation.q: PhCH2OH is treated with PCC to give X. X reacts with CH3MgBr and then aqueous acid to give Y, and Y is treated with Jones reagent to give Z. What is Z?
Which reagents stop at the aldehyde?
Which reagents take a primary alcohol to the acid?
Why does using less Jones reagent not stop at the aldehyde?
A molecule has a primary and a secondary alcohol, and you want only the primary oxidized. What do you do?
You need butan-1-ol converted to butanal in one step, and you have no way to cool a reaction to -78 C. Which reagent?
What intermediate does a chromium oxidation go through?
Which alcohol gives 2-methylpropanal, (CH3)2CHCHO, when treated with Dess-Martin periodinane?
Which alcohol class gives a ketone on oxidation?
You need an aldehyde and the substrate is acid-sensitive. Best choice?
Na2Cr2O7 with H2SO4 behaves most like which reagent?
(R)-Butan-2-ol is oxidized with PCC, and the product is reduced with NaBH4 in methanol. What is isolated?
cis- and trans-4-tert-Butylcyclohexanol are each oxidized with PCC. What do the two flasks contain?
options: Ketone from the trans isomer; the cis isomer does not react

alcohol-oxidation.q: Which statement about secondary alcohols is correct?
options: PCC and Jones give different products

alcohol-oxidation.q: Propose the two-step route from 1-bromobutane to butanoic acid.
options: Jones reagent directly on the bromide
NaOH in water (SN2) to give butan-1-ol, then Jones reagent

alcohol-oxidation.q: Hex-5-en-1-ol (HOCH2CH2CH2CH2CH=CH2) is treated with PCC in CH2Cl2. What is the product?
options: Hexanal - the alkene is reduced as well

alcohol-oxidation.q: An aldehyde in water exists partly as what?
Which is NOT a way to stop at the aldehyde?
Why can a ketone not be oxidized further under these conditions?
options: No hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon

alcohol-oxidation.q: Propan-1-ol (bp 97 C) is oxidized with aqueous Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 while propanal (bp 49 C) is distilled out of the flask as it forms. Why does this give propanal when simply using less oxidant does not?
options: Distillation removes the chromium from the flask
Heating turns Cr(VI) into an anhydrous reagent
The aldehyde leaves the water before it can hydrate

alcohol-oxidation.q: Hexane-1,6-diol is treated with excess Jones reagent. What comes out?
options: No reaction; diols are inert to Cr(VI)

carbonyl-reduction.q: Ethyl 3-oxobutanoate, CH3COCH2CO2CH2CH3, is treated with NaBH4 in ethanol, then worked up. What is the product?
Ethyl 5-oxohexanoate, CH3CO(CH2)3CO2CH2CH3, is treated with excess LiAlH4 in dry THF, then aqueous workup. What organic products are isolated?
What does NaBH4 give from an ester?
What does LiAlH4 give from an ester?
What does LiAlH4 give from an amide?
Ethyl benzoate, PhCO2CH2CH3, is treated with one equivalent of DIBAL-H at -78 C, then aqueous workup. Besides ethanol, what is the main organic product?
N,N-Dimethylbenzamide, PhCON(CH3)2, is treated with LiAlH4, then aqueous workup. What is the product?
What does either hydride reagent do to an isolated alkene?
Why is LiAlH4 more reactive than NaBH4?
options: It is supplied at a much higher concentration
Al is less electronegative, so Al-H is more polarized

carbonyl-reduction.q: Butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2CN, is reduced with LiAlH4 and worked up. What is the product?
Benzoyl chloride, PhCOCl, is treated with excess NaBH4, then worked up. What is the product?
A molecule has a ketone and an ester. To reduce only the ketone, use what?
Why can you not normally stop an ester reduction at the aldehyde?
options: The aldehyde is more electrophilic than the ester
There is no aldehyde intermediate formed at any point

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which reagent can stop an ester at the aldehyde?
4-Acetylbenzoic acid, CH3CO-C6H4-CO2H, is treated with NaBH4 and worked up. What is the product?
What does the Clemmensen reduction do?
options: Reduces C=O to CH2 under acid
Reduces C=O to a plain alcohol

carbonyl-reduction.q: What conditions does the Wolff-Kishner reduction use?
options: LiAlH4 in dry ether at 0 C

carbonyl-reduction.q: A ketone must be converted to a CH2 group in a molecule that also carries an acetal, which has to survive. Which conditions?
Which substrate does NOT give a CH2 group with Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner?
What does NaBH4 give from a carboxylic acid?
Which reagent reduces a nitrile?
A ketone C5H10O is reduced with NaBH4, and the alcohol it gives has no stereocenter. Which ketone was it?
options: Any of them: a ketone reduction never makes a stereocenter

carbonyl-reduction.q: What makes a hydride reduction the same mechanism as a Grignard addition?
options: Both are nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl carbon

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which substrate does NaBH4 NOT reduce?
Cyclohexane-1,4-dione is treated with excess NaBH4. What is the product?
(R)-3-Methylcyclohexanone is reduced with NaBH4. What is the stereochemical outcome?
options: cis and trans alcohols, both R at C3

carbonyl-reduction.q: Supply the reagent: CH3CH2CO2CH3 (methyl propanoate) into CH3CH2CH2OH (propan-1-ol).
options: LiAlH4 in dry THF, then aqueous workup

carbonyl-reduction.q: A molecule contains a ketone, an ester and a terminal alkene. You want the alkene reduced and nothing else. Which reagent?
options: H2 over PtO2 at high pressure

carbonyl-reduction.q: Which two reagents reduce a carboxylic acid?
Butan-2-one is reduced with NaBH4 in methanol, then worked up. What is the product?
options: Butane, by loss of the oxygen

hydrogenation.q: Hex-3-yne is treated with H2 over Lindlar catalyst. What is the product?
Which starting material and conditions give (E)-oct-4-ene?
options: Oct-4-yne with H2 over Lindlar catalyst
Oct-1-yne with Na in liquid NH3
Oct-4-yne with Na in liquid NH3

hydrogenation.q: What is the stereochemistry of catalytic hydrogenation?
Hydrogenating 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene gives what?
1-Nitro-4-vinylbenzene, O2N-C6H4-CH=CH2, is stirred under H2 (1 atm) over Pd/C until no more gas is taken up. What is the product?
What does H2/Pd/C at 1 atm do to a benzene ring?
What does H2/Pd/C do to a nitro group?
What conditions reduce a ketone by hydrogenation?
Methyl (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoate, PhCH=CHCO2CH3, is hydrogenated over Pd/C at 1 atm. What is the product?
What does the Lindlar catalyst give from an alkyne?
A hydrocarbon C6H10 takes up two equivalents of H2 over Pd/C to give hexane. With one equivalent of H2 over Lindlar catalyst it gives (Z)-hex-2-ene. What is it?
What does Na in liquid NH3 give from an alkyne?
Why does Na/NH3 give the trans alkene?
options: The radical anion adopts the less hindered form
The vinyl anion formed after the second electron transfer is configurationally stable and sits with its R groups apart
