Controlling which partner forms the enolate
Only identical carbonyls can ever react together

aldol.q: In a base-catalyzed aldol reaction, the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon of the second molecule is:
options: A free alpha carbanion not stabilized by resonance
The carbonyl oxygen of the first molecule
The enolate formed from the alpha carbon of the first carbonyl compound

aldol.q: The direct product of an aldol addition (before any dehydration) is classified structurally as a:
An aldol addition reaction is reversible under the basic or acidic conditions typically used to carry it out.
Heating an aldol addition product (a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound) under acidic or basic conditions typically leads to:
options: Reduction of the carbonyl to an alcohol
Loss of water (dehydration) to form an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound (an enone)
Formation of a new ring with no change in oxidation state

aldol.q: The overall dehydration step following an aldol addition is favorable largely because the resulting C=C double bond becomes conjugated with the carbonyl group.
Under strongly acidic conditions, the first step of an acid-catalyzed aldol reaction (before enol formation) is:
options: Deprotonation of the alpha carbon by water
Formation of a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate
Direct nucleophilic attack by the unactivated carbonyl compound

aldol.q: The dialdehyde shown is warmed with dilute NaOH. What is the intramolecular aldol condensation product?
options: An open-chain dienal, because a seven-carbon chain cannot reach round on itself

aldol.q: Using an aldehyde that lacks any alpha hydrogens (such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde) together with a ketone that does have alpha hydrogens is a common strategy to favor a clean crossed aldol product.
An intramolecular aldol reaction, used to build rings, is most favorable when it forms a ring of what typical size range?
options: Rings are never formed by intramolecular aldol reactions

aldol.q: A chemist treats an excess of the ketone shown with a catalytic amount of base. What is the immediate aldol addition product before any dehydration?
options: Mesityl oxide directly, with no intermediate

aldol.q: Which best describes why an aldehyde is generally a better electrophile in an aldol reaction than a ketone, all else being equal?
options: Ketones cannot form enolates under any conditions
Its carbonyl carbon is less hindered and less stabilized
Aldehydes are always less acidic at the alpha position than ketones

aldol.q: In a directed (controlled) crossed aldol strategy, a chemist often first converts one carbonyl compound completely into its enolate using a strong base like LDA at low temperature, then adds the second carbonyl compound. Why does this help control the product?
options: It has no effect; the reaction would give the same mixture regardless of addition order
It converts the second carbonyl compound into an enolate automatically
It prevents the aldol reaction from happening at all
Pre-forming one enolate fixes which partner is the nucleophile

aldol.q: An intramolecular aldol condensation of hexanedial (a six-carbon dialdehyde) under basic conditions is a key step used to build which type of product?
options: An open-chain carboxylic acid with no ring
A simple ether with no new carbon-carbon bond
An aromatic benzene ring directly, with no aliphatic intermediate

aldol.q: The retro-aldol reaction (the reverse of aldol addition) is favored by which set of conditions?
options: Only strongly acidic, anhydrous, low-temperature conditions
Dilute base and heat, cleaving the C-C bond to two carbonyls
Conditions identical to those used for a Claisen condensation, with no overlap to aldol chemistry
Only when the aldol product has already been reduced to a diol

aldol.q: A beta-hydroxy ketone that has no hydrogen on the alpha carbon - the one lying between the carbonyl and the hydroxyl-bearing beta carbon - generally cannot undergo the typical E1cb dehydration pathway to give an enone.
Acid-catalyzed dehydration of an aldol product does not pass through a free carbocation. What pushes the protonated beta hydroxyl out as water?
options: An empty p orbital on the carbonyl carbon, overlapping with the beta carbon
Conjugation from the carbonyl, which stabilizes a cation left behind on the beta carbon
The pi electrons of the enol tautomer's C=C, which become the new alpha-beta double bond
A lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen, reaching across the alpha carbon to displace the water

aldol.q: When comparing an aldol addition performed under acidic versus basic conditions, the key mechanistic difference is that the acid-catalyzed pathway proceeds through an enol of the nucleophile, while the base-catalyzed pathway proceeds through a fully formed enolate anion.
Cyclohexanone and 4-methylbenzaldehyde are stirred together with NaOH and heated. What is the major product?
options: A 1:1 mixture of two different crossed aldol products

aldol.q: A student proposes that the aldol reaction and the Claisen condensation are mechanistically identical in every step, including the final fate of the tetrahedral intermediate. Is this correct?
options: No, because the Claisen intermediate expels an alkoxide
Yes, both reactions always end by eliminating water in an identical final step
Yes, both reactions never involve enolate nucleophiles
No, because the aldol reaction does not involve a carbonyl electrophile at all

aldol.q: Explain why treating an unsymmetrical ketone like 2-butanone with base in a self-aldol reaction can, in principle, generate a complex mixture of products even without a second, different carbonyl compound present.
options: 2-Butanone has no alpha hydrogens, so no enolate can form
2-Butanone forms two different enolates, giving several products
Self-aldol reactions never produce more than one possible product in any ketone
Only symmetrical ketones can undergo any enolization at all

aldol.q: In an intramolecular aldol condensation used for ring synthesis, forming a five- or six-membered ring is strongly favored, but if a substrate's connectivity would only allow formation of a strained four-membered or a large, floppy ten-membered ring via the expected enolate/electrophile pairing, what commonly happens?
options: The reaction always proceeds to form the four- or ten-membered ring regardless of strain or entropy cost
No aldol condensation can ever occur if one possible ring size is unfavorable
The alternative enolate or carbonyl reacts, giving a five- or six-membered ring
The carbonyl groups spontaneously swap positions on the molecule to avoid the problem

aldol.q: An aldol product that still has the alpha hydrogen E1cb needs will not dehydrate, even on prolonged heating with base: its carbonyl and beta-hydroxyl sit on a bicyclic framework where the new C=C would have to lie at a bridgehead. What principle is at work?
options: The new alkene would not be conjugated with the carbonyl
Bredt's rule: a small bicyclic system cannot carry a C=C at its bridgehead
Base can promote a substitution but not an elimination
A beta-hydroxy carbonyl needs acid rather than base to lose water

aldol.q: A crossed aldol reaction between an aromatic aldehyde (no alpha hydrogens, such as benzaldehyde) and acetone under basic conditions, followed by dehydration, typically yields which kind of product?
options: A simple reduction product with no new carbon-carbon bond
Benzoic acid as the major product
A product with no conjugation between the new alkene and the ketone

aldol.q: A chemist wants to isolate the aldol addition product (beta-hydroxy ketone) without any dehydration occurring. Which set of conditions is most appropriate?
options: Strong acid at reflux for many hours
Mild base, low temperature, and short reaction time, avoiding heat or strong acid that would drive elimination
Excess base at high temperature for an extended period
Any conditions at all, since dehydration cannot be avoided once an aldol addition occurs

aldol.q: Why is it generally true that an aldol condensation product (the dehydrated enone) cannot undergo a simple retro-aldol reaction to regenerate the original two carbonyl starting materials, even though the initial aldol addition product can.
options: Aldol condensation products never contain any carbonyl group at all
Retro-aldol reactions are only possible for aromatic compounds
Dehydration destroys the beta-hydroxy carbon retro-aldol needs
Elimination reactions are always irreversible under every possible condition, unlike addition reactions

aldol.q: Two equivalents of acetaldehyde undergo a base-catalyzed aldol reaction followed by dehydration. What is the final condensation product?
The enal shown is an aldol condensation product. Which single aldehyde, condensed with itself, gives it?

claisen.q: A Claisen condensation is essentially an aldol-type reaction between two:
options: Esters, where the enolate of one attacks the carbonyl of another

claisen.q: Unlike the aldol reaction, the Claisen condensation product loses a leaving group because:
options: There is no leaving group present
Esters undergo acyl substitution, not simple addition, due to their alkoxy leaving group
Claisen reactions never form a tetrahedral intermediate

claisen.q: What is the key thermodynamic driving force that pulls a Claisen condensation to completion, even though the starting ester enolate equilibrium is unfavorable?
options: The reaction is driven by heat alone
There is no driving force — yields are always low

claisen.q: The classic Claisen condensation of the ester shown with sodium ethoxide produces which well-known beta-ketoester product?
The base typically used in a classic Claisen condensation, such as sodium ethoxide, must match the ester's alkoxy group (for example, NaOEt with an ethyl ester) mainly to avoid:
options: Any possibility of enolate formation occurring at all
The Claisen reaction proceeding too quickly to control
Forming a mixture of products from transesterification if a mismatched alkoxide attacked the ester carbonyl

claisen.q: A Claisen condensation between two molecules of ethyl acetate, when performed with only a catalytic (substoichiometric) amount of sodium ethoxide, can still proceed in good yield to the beta-ketoester product.
To isolate the neutral beta-ketoester product at the end of a Claisen condensation, which final step is necessary?
options: An aqueous acidic workup to protonate the stabilized enolate salt back to the neutral beta-ketoester
No workup is needed; the enolate salt is the final isolable product
Addition of excess sodium ethoxide to drive the reaction further
Heating the enolate salt strongly with no acid present

claisen.q: An ester that has no alpha hydrogens at all, such as ethyl benzoate, can still act as the nucleophile in a Claisen-type condensation by forming its own enolate.
Which intermediate is common to both the aldol reaction and the Claisen condensation mechanism?

In a crossed (mixed) Claisen condensation designed to give a single clean product, one common strategy uses an ester that lacks alpha hydrogens (such as ethyl benzoate or diethyl carbonate) combined with an ester or ketone that does have alpha hydrogens. Why does this help?
options: It guarantees that no Claisen reaction can occur between the two compounds
It forces both compounds to act as nucleophiles simultaneously
The alpha-hydrogen-free partner can only be the electrophile
It eliminates the need for any base catalyst in the reaction

claisen.q: Why is diethyl carbonate, (EtO)2C=O, a useful electrophilic partner in a crossed Claisen-type reaction used to install a -CO2Et (carboethoxy) group onto a ketone's alpha carbon?
options: Diethyl carbonate can only act as a reducing agent, never as an electrophile
Diethyl carbonate has alpha hydrogens that are more acidic than the ketone's
Diethyl carbonate is incapable of undergoing nucleophilic acyl substitution
Diethyl carbonate has two ethoxy leaving groups and no alpha hydrogens

claisen.q: Ethyl acetoacetate (the Claisen condensation product of ethyl acetate) has a pKa for its central CH2 of about 11, much lower than the starting ester's own alpha C-H pKa of about 25. This large acidity increase of the product compared to the starting material is essential to the reaction's success because:
options: It makes the final deprotonation essentially irreversible
It has no real bearing on whether the reaction proceeds to completion
It means the starting ester was never capable of forming an enolate in the first place
It shows that the product is less stable than the starting material

claisen.q: An intramolecular Claisen condensation, known as a Dieckmann condensation, is used to form which type of product?
options: An open-chain diester with no ring formed
A cyclic beta-ketoester, by having one ester's enolate attack a carbonyl carbon within the same molecule
A simple alcohol with no carbonyl remaining
An aromatic ring formed directly from an aliphatic diester with no other changes

claisen.q: If a Claisen condensation is attempted using only enough base to deprotonate a small equilibrium amount of the starting ester's alpha hydrogen, and the beta-ketoester product formed is then immediately and irreversibly removed from the mixture by some means, the reaction can still be driven to high conversion overall.

A mixed Claisen condensation between an ester and a ketone (both bearing alpha hydrogens) is often designed so the ketone's enolate is the nucleophile attacking the ester's carbonyl, rather than the reverse. Why is this the generally preferred direction?
options: Esters can never act as electrophiles under any circumstances
Ketone enolates are incapable of attacking any carbonyl electrophile
Ketone alpha hydrogens are more acidic and esters are better electrophiles
There is no preferred direction; both directions always occur to an identical extent

claisen.q: Why does a Dieckmann condensation typically fail (or give poor yields) when the diester substrate's chain length would force formation of a three- or four-membered ring, or an unusually large ring, upon cyclization?
options: Dieckmann condensations are only capable of forming six-membered rings and no other size under any circumstances
Diesters with short or long chains have no alpha hydrogens at all
The ester groups in such diesters cannot be deprotonated by any base
Ring strain in small rings and entropy in large rings disfavor cyclization

claisen.q: In a Claisen condensation mechanism, after the ester enolate attacks the second ester's carbonyl carbon to form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, what determines whether that intermediate collapses back to reform the two separate ester molecules versus proceeding forward by expelling the alkoxide leaving group to form the beta-ketoester?
options: Both directions are reversible; the irreversible product deprotonation drives it forward
Only the reverse pathway is mechanistically possible at the tetrahedral intermediate stage
The intermediate always instantly and irreversibly collapses only in the forward direction with no possibility of reversal
The choice is determined solely by the temperature of the reaction with no dependence on downstream steps

claisen.q: A student claims that the Claisen condensation can proceed to useful conversion even without any final deprotonation step, as long as enough strong base is used to fully convert the starting ester into its enolate at the outset. Evaluate this claim.
options: This is correct; the final deprotonation step plays no meaningful role in the reaction's success
This is incorrect; full enolate formation supplies no driving force
This is correct, because starting esters are always more acidic than their beta-ketoester products
This is incorrect because esters can never form enolates under any basic conditions

claisen.q: Explain why attempting a Claisen condensation on an ester whose alpha carbon is fully substituted (bearing no alpha hydrogens, such as ethyl trimethylacetate, (CH3)3C-CO2Et) with ethoxide as the only base gives no Claisen condensation product.
options: Ethyl trimethylacetate has no carbonyl group, so it cannot react with any base
Ethoxide is incapable of acting as a nucleophile toward any ester carbonyl
With no alpha hydrogen, the ester cannot form the enolate nucleophile
The reaction would proceed normally and give a Claisen product regardless of alpha-hydrogen availability

claisen.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Dieckmann condensation from an ordinary (intermolecular) Claisen condensation?
options: A Dieckmann condensation never involves an ester enolate as the nucleophile
An ordinary Claisen condensation can only be performed intramolecularly
Dieckmann condensations exclusively use ketones, never esters
A Dieckmann condensation is an intramolecular Claisen forming a ring

claisen.q: Treating diethyl adipate (a six-carbon diester, diethyl hexanedioate) with sodium ethoxide under Dieckmann conditions is expected to give a cyclic beta-ketoester with what typical ring size?
options: No ring at all; only an open-chain product forms

claisen.q: A chemist performs a Claisen condensation and, after the reaction, adds aqueous acid to the mixture but observes that essentially no change in the product occurs beyond simple protonation. What does this indicate about the state of the mixture just before the acidic workup?
options: The acid completely reversed the Claisen condensation back to two molecules of starting ester
The product was already present as its stabilized sodium enolate salt
No reaction had occurred at all prior to the acidic workup
The acid caused a new Claisen condensation to begin for the first time

claisen.q: Which of the following best explains why methyl or ethyl esters are the typical substrates for a Claisen condensation rather than, say, tert-butyl esters?
options: tert-Butyl esters have no carbonyl group and cannot react at all
Methyl and ethyl esters have no alpha hydrogens, unlike tert-butyl esters
Small alkoxy groups leave more readily and match the alkoxide base
Only methyl and ethyl esters are capable of nucleophilic acyl substitution

claisen.q: A Claisen condensation performed using potassium tert-butoxide as the base with an ethyl ester substrate risks a side reaction because:
options: Potassium tert-butoxide cannot remove any alpha hydrogens from an ester
Ethyl esters have no leaving group available under any conditions
tert-Butoxide instantly destroys all carbonyl groups present
tert-Butoxide can attack the carbonyl or transesterify the ester

claisen.q: In a Dieckmann condensation, after the intramolecular ring-closing addition-elimination step gives the cyclic beta-ketoester, what final step (analogous to the intermolecular Claisen condensation) is still required to drive the overall process to completion?
options: Irreversible deprotonation of the cyclic beta-ketoester by alkoxide
Reduction of the new ring to a fully saturated hydrocarbon
Addition of a strong oxidizing agent to complete the mechanism
No further step is needed; ring closure alone is sufficient with no driving force required

claisen.q: A chemist notices that attempting a Claisen condensation on a simple ester using only weak, catalytic amounts of a non-alkoxide base (such as a very weak amine whose conjugate acid pKa is far below that of ethanol) fails to give useful product, even though the final beta-ketoester is quite acidic. What is the most likely reason?
options: Weak bases always deprotonate beta-ketoesters more effectively than alkoxides do
The base is too weak to form the ester enolate
Claisen condensations require no base of any kind to proceed
The ester's carbonyl carbon becomes unreactive in the presence of any weak base

claisen.q: The ester shown is treated with NaOEt and then dilute acid. What is the product?
Which pair of reagents installs a -CO2Et group on the alpha carbon of cyclohexanone in one step?
options: Ethyl acetate with LDA at -78 C

claisen.q: Diethyl pentanedioate (diethyl glutarate) is treated with NaOEt. What happens?
options: It closes a five-membered ring cleanly
It closes a six-membered ring cleanly
The ring it would have to close is four-membered, so essentially none forms
It gives an open-chain beta-ketoester with no ring at all

claisen.q: A beta-ketoester with the skeleton PhCO-CH2-CO2Et is to be made by a crossed Claisen. Which pair of starting materials, with NaOEt, gives it cleanly?

amine-structure.q: Amines are basic because the nitrogen has:
Why are amides far less basic than amines, even though both contain nitrogen?
options: Amide nitrogen has no lone pair at all
There is no difference in basicity

amine-structure.q: Ranking by basicity in water, where does aniline (an aromatic amine) typically fall relative to a simple alkylamine like methylamine?
Amines are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on:
options: the number of hydrogens on nitrogen
the number of lone pairs on nitrogen
the molecular weight of the amine
the number of carbon groups attached to nitrogen

amine-structure.q: What is the approximate geometry around the nitrogen in a typical sp3 amine?
The nitrogen lone pair in an amine is responsible for both its basicity and its nucleophilicity.
Compared to alcohols of similar size, amines generally have:
options: higher boiling points because nitrogen hydrogen-bonds more strongly than oxygen
lower boiling points because N-H bonds hydrogen-bond more weakly than O-H bonds
no hydrogen bonding ability at all

amine-structure.q: Which best describes a quaternary ammonium salt?
options: a tertiary amine that still has a lone pair
an amine bonded to four hydrogens
nitrogen bonded to four carbon groups, permanently positively charged with no lone pair
an amide with four substituents on nitrogen

amine-structure.q: A flask contains cyclohexanone and cyclohexylamine dissolved in diethyl ether. You shake it with 1 M aqueous HCl and separate the layers. Where is each compound?
options: Both stay in the ether layer, since neither one is ionic
Cyclohexylamine moves into the water as its ammonium chloride; the ketone stays in the ether
Cyclohexanone moves into the water as an oxonium salt; the amine stays in the ether
Both move into the water layer, since both have a lone pair to protonate

amine-structure.q: Which functional group definition correctly describes an amine?
options: a carbon bonded to nitrogen through a double bond only
nitrogen directly bonded to a carbonyl carbon
a carbon framework with nitrogen bonded by single bonds and bearing a lone pair

amine-structure.q: When chemists compare amine basicity using pKa values, the pKa listed usually refers to:
Why is methylamine more basic than ammonia in the gas phase and in most basicity comparisons?
options: methyl withdraws electron density, making nitrogen less electron rich
the methyl group inductively donates electron density, helping stabilize the positive charge formed on protonation
methylamine has resonance stabilization that ammonia lacks
ammonia's lone pair is delocalized into an empty orbital

amine-structure.q: Which nitrogen of the amino acid lysine, H2N-CH2CH2CH2CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH, is the more basic?
options: The side-chain NH2 at the far end of the butyl chain
The alpha-NH2 sitting next to the carboxyl group
They are equally basic, since both are primary amines
Neither one is basic, because the COOH protonates both

amine-structure.q: Among methylamine, dimethylamine, and trimethylamine in aqueous solution, dimethylamine is often the most basic overall. What explains this?
options: trimethylamine has resonance stabilization that lowers its basicity
dimethylamine's nitrogen carries two lone pairs
methyl groups withdraw electron density inductively
a balance of alkyl donation against steric/solvation effects

amine-structure.q: In water, trimethylamine is the most basic of the methylamines because it has the most electron-donating methyl groups.
Among pyrrole nitrogen, pyridine nitrogen, and a simple alkylamine nitrogen, which lone pair is least available to accept a proton?
An amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the adjacent carbonyl pi system through resonance. What effect does this have on basicity compared to a simple amine?
options: it increases basicity due to extra resonance stabilization of the protonated amide
it sharply decreases basicity because electron density is pulled toward oxygen
it has essentially no effect on basicity
it makes the amide more basic than ammonia

amine-structure.q: Under strongly acidic conditions, why does protonation of an amide occur preferentially at the carbonyl oxygen rather than at nitrogen?
options: protonating nitrogen gives the more stable cation
oxygen has no lone pairs available so protonation there is actually impossible
the O-protonated cation is resonance-stabilized on O and N
amides are never protonated under any conditions

amine-structure.q: Which order correctly ranks ammonia, methylamine, and aniline from most basic to least basic?
Which substituent, placed para to the amino group on an aniline ring, would make that aromatic amine MORE basic than aniline itself?
options: a strongly electron-withdrawing group such as -NO2
no substituent can increase basicity beyond aniline

amine-structure.q: Adding a nitro group para to the amino group on aniline increases the resulting amine's basicity.
Imidazole (found in histidine) is considerably more basic than pyrrole even though both contain a pyrrole-type nitrogen. What explains this?
options: both nitrogens in imidazole are equally basic and their effects simply add together
imidazole's second nitrogen has an sp2 lone pair outside the pi system
imidazole is not aromatic, unlike pyrrole

amine-structure.q: Guanidine, (H2N)2C=NH, has a conjugate acid pKa of about 13.6, making it far MORE basic than an ordinary alkylamine - even though its lone pairs are delocalized. Why doesn't delocalization lower its basicity the way it does in an amide?
options: Its nitrogens are sp3 hybridized, unlike an amide nitrogen
The resonance stabilizes the protonated cation rather than the neutral base, so it shifts the equilibrium toward protonation
Guanidine has no lone pair available to delocalize in the first place
Delocalization raises basicity in every compound that shows it

amine-structure.q: Which correctly ranks these from MOST to LEAST basic: cyclohexylamine nitrogen, pyridine nitrogen, pyrrole nitrogen, amide nitrogen?
Why is the nitrogen lone pair in a nitrile (R-C triple bond N) much less basic than the lone pair in a typical sp3 amine?
options: the sp lone pair has more s-character
nitrile nitrogen has no lone pair at all
nitrile nitrogen carries a formal positive charge

amine-structure.q: Increasing the s-character of the hybrid orbital that holds a nitrogen lone pair tends to decrease that nitrogen's basicity.

An amine nitrogen is constrained in a small, strained ring (such as aziridine) compared to an open-chain secondary amine with the same substitution pattern. How does this ring strain typically affect basicity?
options: ring strain has no measurable effect on basicity
the strain forces more s-character into the lone pair's orbital, which tends to modestly lower basicity
ring strain always substantially increases basicity
the amine becomes aromatic and basicity is lost entirely

amine-structure.q: Ranking triethylamine, pyridine, aniline, and acetamide from strongest to weakest base, which order is correct?
Because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, amines are generally more basic than comparably substituted alcohols or ethers.
Diisopropylamine is a bulky secondary amine that is a poor nucleophile yet still a reasonably strong base in solution. What best explains this apparent contradiction?
options: bulky amines are never actually basic in solution
steric bulk always increases nucleophilicity toward any electrophile
basicity and nucleophilicity are exactly the same property and cannot differ
basicity is thermodynamic, while nucleophilicity is hindered sterically

amine-reactions.q: Amines commonly act as nucleophiles toward carbonyls, forming which product after loss of water (with aldehydes/ketones)?
When a primary amine reacts with an acyl chloride or ester, the product (after loss of the leaving group) is a(n):
A secondary amine reacting with an aldehyde/ketone (instead of a primary amine) typically forms what kind of product, since it cannot lose a second proton from nitrogen to form a C=N?
When a primary amine reacts with excess methyl iodide, the ultimate product after repeated alkylation is:
options: a secondary amine only, with no further reaction

amine-reactions.q: Amines react with strong acids such as HCl to form:
The amine shown is treated with (1) excess CH3I, then (2) acetic anhydride. What is the outcome?
options: An amide forms in step 2, as it would with the free amine
Nothing happens in step 2 - step 1 already destroyed the nucleophile
A second quaternary salt forms in step 2, using the anhydride
An imine forms in step 2 from one of the carbonyl groups

amine-reactions.q: Treating a primary or secondary amine with an acyl chloride (R-COCl) gives which product?
Reacting a primary amine with nitrous acid (HNO2) at low temperature generates a reactive intermediate known as a:
Aryl diazonium salts (made from aromatic primary amines plus HNO2) are stable enough to be isolated and stored at room temperature for long periods.
Direct SN2 alkylation of ammonia or a primary amine with an unactivated alkyl halide is often a poor way to make a single clean product because:
options: amines have no nucleophilic character whatsoever
amines react only with acids, never with alkyl halides
steric hindrance makes even the first alkylation impossible
over-alkylation gives a mixture of alkylated products

amine-reactions.q: When converting an amine to an amide using an acyl chloride, chemists commonly add a base like pyridine or triethylamine mainly to:
options: neutralize the HCl byproduct generated during the reaction
act as the solvent and nothing else

amine-reactions.q: A primary amine condenses with an aldehyde, losing water to form R2C=N-R'. What is this type of product commonly called?
A secondary amine reacting with a ketone forms an enamine instead of an imine. Why?
options: secondary amines cannot bond to carbonyl carbons at all
the carbonyl oxygen remains attached in the final product
with no second N-H, dehydration removes an alpha proton
enamines can only form from primary amines, not secondary ones

amine-reactions.q: Before any water is lost, an amine first adds to an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl to give a tetrahedral intermediate commonly called a:
Tertiary amines can form stable, isolable imines or enamines when reacted with ketones, because nitrogen still has a lone pair available.
You need to convert the ketone shown plus methylamine into N-methylbutan-2-amine, CH3CH2CH(NHCH3)CH3. Which reagent completes the job?
options: NaBH3CN at pH 4-5, in the same flask
LiAlH4 in dry ether, added before the amine
Br2 and NaOH, followed by aqueous workup
Excess CH3I, followed by mild warming

amine-reactions.q: Put the steps of imine formation in order: (i) loss of water, (ii) protonation of the OH, (iii) attack by nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon, (iv) loss of a proton from nitrogen, (v) proton transfer giving the hemiaminal.
Primary aliphatic diazonium salts (from alkylamine plus HNO2) are extremely unstable and rapidly decompose with loss of what gas?
Aryl diazonium salts are synthetically valuable mainly because the N2+ group on the ring can be replaced to give:
options: alcohols exclusively, with no other possible products
phenols, aryl halides, and nitriles, among other substituted aromatics

amine-reactions.q: Reductive amination of a ketone with a primary amine and a reducing agent such as sodium cyanoborohydride is useful because it:
options: converts imine to amine in one pot
only works when the amine is tertiary
produces an amide rather than an amine
requires no reduction step at all

amine-reactions.q: The Gabriel synthesis produces pure primary amines without contamination by secondary or tertiary amines, unlike a direct SN2 alkylation of ammonia.
Which reagent reduces an amide all the way to the corresponding primary amine, removing the carbonyl oxygen entirely?
A chemist treats a tertiary amine with excess acetic anhydride, expecting amide formation. What actually happens at that nitrogen?
options: the tertiary amine forms a stable, isolable tertiary amide
the tertiary amine is simply oxidized by the anhydride
no stable amide forms without an N-H to lose
an ester forms instead of any nitrogen-containing product

amine-reactions.q: In the Gabriel synthesis, after an alkyl halide reacts with potassium phthalimide, what is the purpose of the subsequent hydrazine (or strong hydrolysis) step?
options: it reduces the alkyl group attached to nitrogen
it converts the intermediate into a diazonium salt
it simply regenerates the original alkyl halide
it cleaves the C-N bonds, releasing the amine

amine-reactions.q: Aromatic primary amines react with HNO2 to give diazonium salts that can be briefly used cold, while aliphatic primary amines give diazonium salts that decompose almost instantly even near 0 degrees C. What explains the difference?
options: the aryl diazonium cation is resonance-stabilized by the ring
aliphatic amines simply do not react with HNO2 under any conditions
aryl diazonium salts carry no positive charge, unlike alkyl diazonium salts
alkyl substituents stabilize diazonium ions better than aryl rings do

amine-reactions.q: Secondary amines reacting with nitrous acid form stable N-nitrosamines (R2N-NO) rather than diazonium salts, because they lack a second N-H to lose after the initial nitrosation step.
During reductive amination of a ketone with a primary amine at mildly acidic pH, why is sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH3CN) preferred over sodium borohydride (NaBH4)?
options: NaBH4 is chemically incapable of reducing anything in this system
NaBH3CN reduces the iminium selectively over the ketone
NaBH3CN is preferred purely for being less toxic, with no selectivity advantage
NaBH3CN reduces amides but leaves imines untouched

amine-reactions.q: An amine is treated with excess alkyl halide in a classic direct SN2 alkylation. Even with careful stoichiometry, why doesn't the reaction stop cleanly at the secondary amine stage?

all of the alkyl halide is consumed irreversibly by the very first equivalent of amine present
each alkylation product is still nucleophilic and reacts further, giving a mixture
careful stoichiometry alone always guarantees a clean, single alkylation product

amine-reactions.q: Diazotization needs acid, and it needs a primary amine. What does each requirement do?

The acid reduces the nitrogen to its -3 oxidation level, and a primary amine is simply the cheapest starting material
The acid supplies the nitrogen that ends up in the N2 group, and a primary amine is the least hindered of the three

amine-reactions.q: A primary amine is treated with one equivalent of an acid chloride in the presence of excess pyridine as a base. What roles does pyridine play, and why is it chosen over a strong base like NaOH?

pyridine acts purely as a reducing agent in this reaction
pyridine itself becomes incorporated into the amide product
pyridine serves only as an inert solvent with no chemical role

aromaticity.q: For a ring system to be aromatic, it must be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and have how many pi electrons (by Hückel’s rule)?

aromaticity.q: Is the cyclopentadienyl cation (4 pi electrons, planar, cyclic) aromatic, anti-aromatic, or non-aromatic?

options: Both aromatic; the counts settle it

aromaticity.q: Benzene satisfies Hückel's rule with 6 pi electrons corresponding to n = 2 in the 4n+2 formula.

options: It has too few pi electrons

Is the cyclopropenyl cation (a three-membered ring with 2 pi electrons, planar and fully conjugated) aromatic?
options: No, because the ring is too small to be aromatic
No, because cations can never be aromatic
Yes, but only in nonpolar solvents
Yes, because 2 pi electrons fits 4n+2 with n = 0

aromaticity.q: Pyridine's nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, so it does not participate in the aromatic pi system.

options: It contributes one lone pair (2 electrons) into the ring's pi system
It contributes zero electrons; both lone pairs stay out of plane
It contributes both lone pairs (4 electrons) into the ring's pi system
Oxygen cannot be part of an aromatic ring

aromaticity.q: Rank cyclopentadiene, the cyclopentadienyl cation, and the cyclopentadienyl anion from most to least stable relative to a typical non-aromatic comparison.

Which species below is classified as antiaromatic?

A compound is planar, cyclic, and fully conjugated with 8 pi electrons. What is its classification?

options: No, because full conjugation is also required
Yes, the electron count alone guarantees aromaticity
Yes, as long as it is planar
No, because 6 is never a valid pi electron count

aromaticity.q: Cyclobutadiene's high reactivity is explained by calling it non-aromatic: it is simply an ordinary, unstabilized diene.
Why does the aromatic stabilization of benzene show up experimentally as a lower-than-expected heat of hydrogenation?
options: Because benzene has fewer hydrogens than expected
Because the delocalized pi system is lower in energy
Because benzene reacts faster with hydrogen than cyclohexene
Because hydrogenation of benzene is endothermic

aromaticity.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes non-aromatic from antiaromatic compounds?
options: Non-aromatic compounds are less stable than antiaromatic compounds
Antiaromatic compounds fail to meet the planarity or conjugation requirement, while non-aromatic compounds meet the 4n+2 rule
Non-aromatic compounds miss a structural requirement; antiaromatic ones meet them all but have 4n pi electrons
There is no meaningful distinction between the two terms

aromaticity.q: Cyclooctatetraene dianion (with 2 extra electrons added, giving 10 pi electrons total, planar) would be predicted to be aromatic.
What structural feature allows benzene's six carbon-carbon bonds to all have the same intermediate length (between single and double bond length) rather than alternating short and long?
options: Benzene's bonds are all single bonds
Benzene is not actually a planar hexagon
Resonance delocalization spreads the pi electron density evenly around the ring

aromaticity.q: Thiophene's sulfur contributes both of its lone pairs to the aromatic pi system, giving 8 pi electrons in total.
A large annulene has 4n+2 pi electrons but is too strained to stay planar. What happens to its aromaticity?
options: It is lost, because planarity is required
It remains perfectly aromatic regardless of size
Ring size has no effect on aromaticity at all

aromaticity.q: Which best explains why the cyclopentadienyl anion is far easier to form than a typical alkyl carbanion?
options: The five-membered ring is less sterically strained
The anion formed is aromatic (6 pi electrons)
Carbon is more electronegative in a ring
The anion is actually less stable, not more

6 — the C=C, the C=N, and N1's lone pair in a p orbital

10 — every lone pair on both nitrogens is counted in

Formation of the resonance-stabilized cationic (arenium) intermediate

options: 1-chlorobutane with AlCl₃, in a single step
butanoic acid with H₂SO₄ and gentle heating
1-butene with HBr, then AlCl₃ and benzene

eas.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl3 in order to generate a reactive carbocation electrophile from an alkyl halide.

options: An acylium ion (R-C triple bond O+ stabilized by resonance)

What is the electrophile in aromatic sulfonation using fuming sulfuric acid?
options: H2SO4 itself acting directly as the electrophile

eas.q: Halogenation of benzene with Br₂ proceeds readily without any catalyst, because benzene's pi system is a stronger nucleophile than an alkene's.

Because aromatic rings cannot react with rearranged cations

options: Because acylation does not involve a carbocation intermediate at all
Because acyl groups are less reactive than alkyl groups
Because resonance-stabilized acylium ions do not rearrange
Because acylation only works on deactivated rings

options: Because alkyl halides are always used in large excess
Because the catalyst is consumed after one substitution
Because alkylated rings are less soluble and precipitate unreacted
Because the added alkyl group activates the ring further

eas.q: Which statement correctly describes why EAS reactions are favorable overall despite requiring a high-energy intermediate?
options: The slow first step is pulled forward by fast rearomatization
The rate-determining step is highly exothermic
EAS reactions do not actually require activation energy
The electrophile is consumed irreversibly before the ring ever reacts

eas.q: In iodination of benzene, an oxidizing agent is typically needed because I2 alone is too weak an electrophile and the reaction is otherwise reversible.
Which reagent or condition removes an –SO₃H group from a benzene ring, and why is that worth having?

Hot dilute aqueous H₂SO₄, because sulfonation is reversible
LiAlH₄, which reduces the sulfonic acid group straight off
Nothing removes it — sulfonation is permanent once it is done

eas.q: Which of the following is the correct overall electrophile sequence in generating the nitronium ion from nitric acid and sulfuric acid?
options: HNO3 is deprotonated by H2SO4, then loses OH- to form NO2+
H2SO4 reacts directly with benzene, and HNO3 is a spectator
HNO3 is protonated by H2SO4 to form H2NO3+, which then loses water to form NO2+

eas.q: Why can EAS reactions be run on benzene derivatives but the aromatic ring never acts as a nucleophile toward a simple alkyl halide without a Lewis acid catalyst present (e.g., plain 1-chlorobutane and benzene alone)?

AlCl3 does not work with nitro-substituted rings for unrelated solubility reasons
Methyl chloride cannot ever be used in Friedel-Crafts alkylation

Because sulfonic acid groups cannot be removed once installed

Halogens have no real electronic effect and the pattern is coincidental
Halogens only deactivate and do not direct at all

Exclusively para-nitrotoluene with no ortho product
Equal amounts of ortho, meta, and para

options: Equally distributed among all three positions

Position 5, the position meta to both of the methyl groups

Induction donates strongly while resonance withdraws strongly
Neither induction nor resonance has any measurable effect

options: Aldehyde protons are attached to a different element than carbon
Vinyl protons are always shielded completely
Deshielding by the carbonyl oxygen and C=O anisotropy
There is no real difference between the two shifts

h-nmr.q: Hydroxyl (O-H) and amine (N-H) proton signals in ¹H NMR are often broader and appear at less predictable chemical shifts than typical C-H signals mainly because:
options: They are always the most intense peaks in the spectrum
They never couple to any other protons under any conditions
They only appear in samples run at very high temperature
They exchange rapidly with trace water

h-nmr.q: A compound C₄H₈O shows ¹H NMR signals at 9.8 ppm (1H, triplet), 2.4 ppm (2H, multiplet), 1.7 ppm (2H, sextet) and 0.95 ppm (3H, triplet). Which structure fits?
Methyl but-2-enoate, CH₃CH=CHCO₂CH₃, shows its two vinyl hydrogens at 6.95 and 5.85 ppm, coupled to each other with J = 15.6 Hz. Which isomer is it?
options: The Z isomer: 15.6 Hz is a cis coupling
Either: J does not depend on geometry
A 1:1 mixture of E and Z
The E isomer: 15.6 Hz is a trans coupling

h-nmr.q: A compound of formula C₉H₁₀O₂ gives a ¹H NMR with four signals: 8.0 ppm (2H, d, J = 8 Hz), 7.3 ppm (2H, d, J = 8 Hz), 3.9 ppm (3H, s), 2.4 ppm (3H, s). Its IR has a strong band at 1720 cm⁻¹ and nothing above 3100. What is the structure?
Comparing CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, and CHCl3, the chemical shift of the carbon-bound proton(s) moves progressively further downfield as the number of chlorine atoms increases. This trend is best explained by:
options: More chlorine atoms make the molecule heavier, which directly shifts the signal downfield
Each added chlorine withdraws more density, increasing deshielding
Chlorine atoms decouple the protons from each other
The trend is actually reversed; more chlorine shifts the signal upfield

h-nmr.q: A compound C₃H₆O₂ shows ¹H NMR signals at 11.8 ppm (1H, broad singlet, gone after a D₂O shake), 2.4 ppm (2H, quartet) and 1.2 ppm (3H, triplet). Which structure fits?
For an ethyl bromide fragment, CH3-CH2-Br, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting pattern for the two proton environments?
options: The CH3 appears as a singlet and the CH2 as a singlet
The CH3 appears as a quartet and the CH2 as a triplet
The CH3 appears as a triplet and the CH2 as a quartet

h-nmr.q: Two protons on the same carbon can be diastereotopic and show different chemical shifts if replacing each one individually (in turn) with a test group would create distinguishable stereochemical outcomes.

A terminal alkyne's C-H proton typically appears around 1.8-3.0 ppm, noticeably more upfield than a typical vinyl proton (around 4.5-6.5 ppm), even though the alkyne carbon is more electronegative (more s-character). This is best explained by:
options: Anisotropic shielding along the triple bond axis
The alkyne has no electronic effects on its proton at all
Alkyne protons are not actually attached to carbon
Vinyl protons are always more shielded than any other type

h-nmr.q: Vinyl (alkene) protons typically appear downfield, around 4.5-6.5 ppm, compared to ordinary alkyl protons. This is mainly due to:
options: Vinyl protons having a different number of neutrons
Anisotropic deshielding by the pi electrons
A simple increase in molecular weight near the double bond
Vinyl protons never experiencing any magnetic effects

h-nmr.q: A highly symmetric molecule like tert-butanol, (CH3)3C-OH, shows how many distinct ¹H NMR signals?
An alkyl bromide shows two ¹H NMR signals: 4.2 ppm (1H, septet) and 1.7 ppm (6H, doublet). Which structure fits?
Protons that are chemically equivalent to each other by molecular symmetry do not produce visible splitting from coupling to one another.
Why does adding a drop of D2O to an NMR sample often cause an O-H or N-H peak to shrink or disappear from the ¹H NMR spectrum?
options: The O-H or N-H proton exchanges with deuterium from D2O
D2O reacts chemically with the carbon skeleton of the molecule
D2O always increases the intensity of every peak in the spectrum

h-nmr.q: For an isopropyl group, -CH(CH3)2, attached to a larger chain, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting for the central CH proton and the two equivalent CH3 groups?
options: The CH appears as a doublet and the CH3 groups appear as a septet
The CH appears as a septet and the CH3 groups appear as a doublet
The CH appears as a quartet and the CH3 groups appear as a triplet

h-nmr.q: A CH2 group flanked by a stereocenter elsewhere in the molecule can show an unusually complicated splitting pattern (such as an ABX-type pattern) rather than a simple doublet, because:
options: CH2 groups can never show splitting of any kind
The molecule must contain a triple bond nearby
This pattern only happens in aromatic rings

h-nmr.q: The simple n+1 rule for predicting splitting patterns assumes that a proton couples equally (with the same coupling constant) to all of its neighboring protons; when neighboring protons have noticeably different coupling constants, more complex multiplets than the simple n+1 prediction can result.

Rank the following methyl groups from most upfield to most downfield based on typical ¹H NMR chemical shift: CH3 attached to a plain alkyl carbon, CH3 attached to a carbonyl (as in a methyl ketone), CH3 attached directly to an aromatic ring, CH3 attached to an oxygen (as in a methyl ether).
options: Alkyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then O-CH3
O-CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then alkyl CH3
Aromatic CH3, then alkyl CH3, then O-CH3, then carbonyl CH3
Alkyl CH3, then carbonyl CH3, then aromatic CH3, then O-CH3

h-nmr.q: Why do long-range couplings across four or more bonds usually fail to produce visible splitting in a routine ¹H NMR spectrum of a simple flexible molecule?
options: Coupling constants fall off sharply beyond three bonds
Long-range coupling is physically impossible under any circumstances
Only aromatic rings are capable of long-range coupling
Splitting always increases without limit as more bonds are added

h-nmr.q: An ethanol sample's O-H proton integrates to 1H in theory, but the measured integration can vary noticeably between samples and conditions. The most likely explanation is:
options: The molecular formula of ethanol changes between samples
The O-H proton exchanges with trace water
O-H protons never integrate correctly under any circumstances
Ethanol does not actually contain an O-H proton

h-nmr.q: A proton held directly above the face of a benzene ring in a rigid molecule appears at 0.5 ppm, upfield of an ordinary alkane proton, while the protons on the ring's edge appear at 7.3 ppm. What does this pair of observations establish?
options: That chemical shift is fixed by the electronegativity of nearby atoms alone
That chemical shift depends on where a proton sits relative to a nearby pi system
That the rigid molecule has to be measured on a different spectrometer entirely
That protons above a ring and protons on its edge are chemically identical

h-nmr.q: Two protons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry within an otherwise achiral, conformationally averaged molecule will typically give the same ¹H NMR chemical shift.

In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, peak height or area reliably indicates the number of carbons contributing to that signal, the same way integration works in ¹H NMR.
An aromatic compound C₈H₁₀ shows six ¹³C signals, and one of them points down in DEPT-135. Which structure fits?
A compound C₅H₁₀O shows five ¹³C signals, including one at 209 ppm that is absent from DEPT-135. Which structure fits?
A compound C₈H₈O₂ shows six ¹³C signals: 191, 164, 132, 130, 114 and 55 ppm. In DEPT-135, 191, 132, 114 and 55 point up; 164 and 130 are absent. Which structure fits?
A ketone's carbonyl carbon (around 205-220 ppm) appears at a higher chemical shift than an ester's carbonyl carbon (around 165-175 ppm). This difference is mainly explained by:
options: Esters contain no carbonyl carbon at all
The alkoxy oxygen shields it by resonance
Ketones always have more carbons overall
The difference is purely due to molecular weight

c-nmr.q: Alkyne carbons typically appear around 65-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, noticeably more upfield than alkene or aromatic carbons (roughly 100-150 ppm), even though all are unsaturated. The best explanation is:
options: Alkyne carbons have no electronic effects on their chemical shift
Alkynes never appear in ¹³C NMR spectra
Alkyne carbons are always attached to oxygen

c-nmr.q: Because of its molecular symmetry, how many distinct ¹³C NMR signals would toluene (methylbenzene) show, given that the ring carbons pair up by symmetry?
In a DEPT experiment, quaternary carbons (carbons with no attached hydrogens) are distinguished from CH, CH2, and CH3 carbons because:
options: Quaternary carbons vanish; DEPT needs attached hydrogens
Quaternary carbons always appear as the tallest peaks in DEPT
DEPT can only detect quaternary carbons and nothing else
Quaternary carbons are shown in a completely different color on the spectrum

c-nmr.q: Quaternary carbons typically show weaker peak intensities in a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum compared to protonated carbons of similar abundance.
Between a simple aldehyde's carbonyl carbon and a simple ketone's carbonyl carbon, which is generally found further downfield in ¹³C NMR?
options: The aldehyde carbonyl carbon is always further downfield
The ketone carbonyl carbon is further downfield
They are always identical in shift
Aldehydes have no carbonyl carbon at all

c-nmr.q: A hydrocarbon C₄H₆ shows two ¹³C signals: about 75 ppm (absent from DEPT-135) and 3 ppm (pointing up). Which structure fits?
Two carbons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry in an achiral molecule will typically give the same ¹³C NMR chemical shift.
A carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon (roughly 170-185 ppm) and an ester's carbonyl carbon (roughly 165-175 ppm) can sometimes be distinguished mainly by:
options: Carboxylic acids never show a carbonyl carbon signal
Esters always appear further downfield than carboxylic acids
There is no possible way to distinguish the two by any NMR method
Their overlapping shift ranges plus the O-H signature

c-nmr.q: A nitrile carbon (C of a C≡N group) typically appears around 115-120 ppm in ¹³C NMR, a range that must be interpreted carefully because:
options: It overlaps the aromatic and alkene region instead of standing clear of it
Nitrile carbons are never detectable by ¹³C NMR
This range is identical to a typical aldehyde carbonyl carbon
Nitrile carbons overlap exactly with the TMS reference signal at zero ppm

c-nmr.q: A para-disubstituted benzene ring with two different substituents, which breaks the ring's six-fold symmetry down to a single mirror plane, would be expected to show how many distinct aromatic ¹³C signals?
Why do we not typically observe carbon-carbon (¹³C-¹³C) spin coupling in a routine ¹³C NMR spectrum, even though carbons are directly bonded to each other throughout the molecule?
options: Carbon-carbon bonds are incapable of transmitting any spin coupling
All carbon-carbon coupling constants are zero by definition
Two bonded carbons are almost never both ¹³C
The decoupler used for proton decoupling also removes all carbon-carbon coupling

c-nmr.q: A molecule can sometimes show a different total number of distinct ¹H NMR signals than distinct ¹³C NMR signals for the same structure. What is one reasonable explanation for this?
options: The two techniques must always give exactly the same number of signals for any molecule
¹³C NMR always shows more signals than ¹H NMR for every molecule
¹H NMR cannot show more than one signal per molecule
Coincidental overlap, or symmetry that equates protons but not carbons

c-nmr.q: In a DEPT-135 experiment, CH and CH3 carbons appear as positive peaks, CH2 carbons appear as negative (inverted) peaks, and quaternary carbons are absent altogether. This pattern is useful mainly because it allows chemists to:
options: Tell how many hydrogens each carbon bears
Directly count the total number of hydrogens in the molecule
Measure the exact bond angles in the molecule

c-nmr.q: ¹³C NMR chemical shifts generally follow the same electronegativity-based deshielding trends seen in ¹H NMR, where attaching a more electronegative atom shifts the signal downfield, though the magnitude of the shift differs between the two techniques.
Neopentane, (CH3)4C, has five carbon atoms but shows only two signals in ¹³C NMR. This is best explained by:
options: Neopentane actually contains only two carbon atoms
Symmetry makes the four methyl carbons equivalent
¹³C NMR cannot detect quaternary carbons under any circumstances
The four methyl groups are not actually bonded to the central carbon

c-nmr.q: Obtaining a good ¹³C NMR spectrum often requires longer acquisition times or more scans rather than simply increasing sample concentration, partly because:
options: ¹³C nuclei are immune to any relaxation effects
Increasing concentration always fully compensates for ¹³C's low natural abundance with no need for extra scans
Long relaxation times, especially for quaternary carbons, require signal averaging over many scans
Longer scans have no effect on signal-to-noise ratio

c-nmr.q: A ¹³C spectrum of a compound with one oxygen-bearing functional group has its most downfield signal at 171 ppm and nothing at all between 186 and 220 ppm. What does that pair of observations establish about the carbonyl?
options: It is a ketone, because ketone carbonyl carbons are the ones that sit lowest, near 165–185
It is an aldehyde, because the attached hydrogen shields that carbon into the 165–185 window
Nothing is narrowed: ketone, aldehyde and ester carbonyls all share the 165–185 window
It is an acid derivative — ester, acid or amide — with heteroatom donation holding it near 165–185

c-nmr.q: In ¹³C NMR, a carbon's chemical shift is strongly affected by nearby electronegative atoms even two or three bonds away, similar to the pattern seen in ¹H NMR, though the size of the effect attenuates with distance in both techniques.

A ketone C₆H₁₂O (M⁺ = 100) shows a base peak at m/z 43 and a strong even-mass peak at m/z 58. Which structure fits?
The molecular ion peak (M+) always corresponds to the most intense peak in the entire mass spectrum.
The relative height of the M+1 isotope peak compared to M+ in a mass spectrum is mainly useful for estimating:
options: The number of nitrogen atoms in the molecule
The approximate number of carbon atoms
The boiling point of the compound
The number of oxygen atoms in the molecule

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single chlorine atom typically shows an M+2 peak with what approximate relative intensity compared to M+?
options: About 10 times the intensity of M+

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single bromine atom typically shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly what relative intensity to each other?
options: M+2 is about ten times more intense than M+
Roughly equal intensity, close to a 1:1 ratio

mass-spec.q: Loss of a methyl radical, corresponding to a mass loss of 15 units, from the molecular ion is a common fragmentation for branched alkyl compounds.
An aromatic hydrocarbon C₉H₁₂ (M⁺ = 120) shows its base peak at m/z 91. Which structure fits?

The nitrogen rule states that, for typical organic compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and similar common elements, the molecular weight will be odd if the molecule contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms.
A loss of 28 mass units from a molecular ion is ambiguous on its own because it could correspond to either:
options: Loss of water or loss of ammonia
Loss of carbon monoxide (CO) or loss of ethylene (C2H4)
Loss of chlorine or loss of bromine
Loss of a proton or loss of a methyl group

mass-spec.q: Alpha cleavage, the preferential breaking of a bond adjacent to a heteroatom such as nitrogen or oxygen, is a favorable fragmentation pathway mainly because:
options: Alpha cleavage never actually occurs in real spectra
Breaking bonds near heteroatoms requires less energy than breaking any other bond in the molecule under all circumstances
The resulting cation can be stabilized by resonance donation from the heteroatom's lone pair
Heteroatoms always prevent any fragmentation nearby

mass-spec.q: A McLafferty rearrangement in a carbonyl-containing compound requires the presence of what structural feature, and produces what kind of products?
options: Any aromatic ring, producing two radical fragments
A triple bond anywhere in the molecule, producing a gas
A halogen atom, producing an odd-electron radical cation only
A gamma-hydrogen, producing an ion and a neutral alkene

mass-spec.q: The characteristic tropylium cation at m/z 91 is commonly observed in the mass spectra of which class of compounds?
options: Primary amines with no ring present

mass-spec.q: More highly branched alkanes generally show a weaker molecular ion peak than their straight-chain isomers, because branching provides additional, more easily accessible fragmentation pathways that generate more stable carbocations.
A loss of 43 mass units from a molecular ion commonly corresponds to loss of which fragment(s)?
In the mass spectrum of a simple aldehyde, a loss of 29 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly corresponds to loss of:
Aromatic compounds often show a strong, easily recognized molecular ion peak relative to many aliphatic compounds mainly because:
options: Aromatic compounds never undergo any fragmentation at all
Aromatic rings always weigh less than aliphatic chains
Aromatic compounds cannot be ionized by electron ionization
Ring delocalization stabilizes the radical cation

mass-spec.q: An unknown shows a molecular ion at m/z 120 with an M+1 peak about 8.8% as tall, no M+2 of any significance, a base peak at m/z 105, and a further strong fragment at m/z 77. Its IR has a strong band at 1690 cm⁻¹ and nothing above 3100 cm⁻¹. What is the structure?
An alcohol C₄H₁₀O gives a weak M⁺ at m/z 74 and its base peak at m/z 31. Which structure fits?

This pattern is most consistent with a ketone structure in which:
options: The molecule contains no carbonyl group at all
The carbonyl is flanked by a methyl and an ethyl group, as in 2-butanone
The molecule must be a symmetrical ketone with identical groups on both sides of the carbonyl
The molecule is necessarily an aromatic compound

mass-spec.q: An unknown gives M⁺ at m/z 88, with an M+1 peak about 4.5% as tall. Its IR shows a very broad band from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong band at 1710 cm⁻¹. Which structure fits?

A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish between two different molecular formulas that share the same nominal (whole-number) mass, such as C2H4O and CO2, both of which equal 44 to the nearest whole number. This is possible because:
options: All atoms have exactly the same mass, so this distinction is actually impossible
High-resolution instruments simply guess the formula from the compound's color
Nominal mass and exact mass are always identical for every molecule
Different atom combinations have slightly different exact masses

mass-spec.q: A mass spectrum shows molecular-ion peaks at m/z 112, 114 and 116 in a 9:6:1 ratio. Which structure fits?

options: The molecular ion can fragment by more than one competing pathway
A molecule can only ever show exactly one fragmentation pathway in its entire spectrum
Loss of water and loss of ethylene must always occur together as a single simultaneous event

options: The compound must contain an even number of nitrogen atoms
The compound cannot contain any nitrogen at all
